Grammar:

- בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים is a construct chain with a plural noun in the absolute and the article; the sense of אֱלֹהִים is the main difficulty.
- כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה is a verbless clause: 'that they were good'. The feminine pronoun הֵנָּה refers to the daughters.
- וַיִּקְחוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים: 'took for themselves women', the idiom for marrying.
- מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּחָרוּ is 'from all whom they chose' (all that they chose); Rashi and Radak read it as including women already married.

Note: Per decisions, אֱלֹהִים of beings other than the God of Israel takes the sense of the normative commentators. Here they differ. Rashi's first reading, with Onkelos (בני רברביא), Ramban and Radak, is 'the sons of the princes and judges' (Rashi: every אֱלֹהִים in Scripture is an expression of authority), and Ibn Ezra lists it first; the English follows Rashi. Rashi's other reading (the angelic princes who go on God's errands) and Ibn Ezra's others (the holy ones; the sons of Seth; and his own preference, those who knew the knowledge of the Most High and chose their wives by the order of the heavens) are recorded below. The Hebrew טֹבֹת is spelled defectively; Rashi's homily from the spelling is not an issue for the plain sense.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים are the sons of the princes and judges; every אֱלֹהִים in Scripture is an expression of authority (cf. Ex 4:16, 7:1). His second reading, the officers who go on God's mission mingling with them, is recorded.
- Rashi (records): Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): טבת is written, 'they made her good': they adorned the bride for the wedding canopy and the great one went in first. A homily on the spelling; the English keeps the plain 'beautiful'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'from all whom they chose' includes even a married woman, even male and beast. The English leaves the extent as in the Hebrew.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra lists readings of בני האלהים: the sons of the judges, who did God's justice on earth; some say that אלהים here means 'holy' and the sons are the holy ones, as in 'you are children' (Dt 14:1); some say the sons of Seth, the daughters being of Cain's family. 'The right in my eyes' (והישר בעיני) is that they were those who knew the knowledge of the Most High and chose wives whose configuration of the heavens matched each man, so that their offspring were like the begetting, and mighty men came from them; they may also have taken the women by force. The English follows Rashi's 'rulers', the first reading Ibn Ezra lists, not his preference.
- Ramban (follows): Ramban: the sons of princes and judges; they did violence openly with no one to restrain them.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: 'כי טובות הנה' means that wherever they were good they took them by force.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the sons of the judges and the great, who are called אֱלֹהִים (Ex 22:27); so Onkelos, בני רברביא. The Midrash on Azza and Azael is far off.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak (Bereshit Rabbah): comments on the long lives of these generations.
- Radak (records): Radak: בנות האדם are the daughters of the common, weak people, who could not resist; he cites Ibn Ezra's different reading.
- Radak (records): Radak (quoting Ibn Ezra): the sons of God were those who knew the Most High and chose by the order of the heavens.
- Radak (records): Radak: the Bereshit Rabbah homily on טבת, 'these are the virgins'.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'took wives' means married women.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'all that they chose' includes male and beast.

Apparatus:

- אֱלֹהִים here: rulers or judges (Rashi's first reading, the first Ibn Ezra lists, Ramban, Radak, Onkelos בני רברביא); the angelic princes who go on God's errands (Rashi's other reading; Radak calls the midrash of Azza and Azael far-fetched); 'the holy ones' (reported by Ibn Ezra); the sons of Seth, with the daughters of Cain's line (reported by Ibn Ezra); those who knew the knowledge of the Most High and chose their wives by the order of the heavens (Ibn Ezra's own preference, quoted by Radak).
- Onkelos renders טֹבֹת with שַׁפִּירָן, 'beautiful'.
- בָּחָרוּ: Onkelos has דִּי אִתְרְעִיאוּ, 'whom they desired'.

#### Genesis 6:3

> וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהֹוָ֗ה לֹֽא־יָד֨וֹן רוּחִ֤י בָֽאָדָם֙ לְעֹלָ֔ם בְּשַׁגַּ֖ם ה֣וּא בָשָׂ֑ר וְהָי֣וּ יָמָ֔יו מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֖ים שָׁנָֽה׃

**Then the LORD said, "My spirit will not contend over humankind for long, since they are also flesh; their days will be one hundred and twenty years."**

Literal: and-said the-LORD not will-contend my-spirit in-the-human for-ever in-since-also he flesh and-will-be his-days hundred and-twenty year

Grammar:

- יָדוֹן is a rare and disputed form. Rashi: it means 'quarrel, contend' (he speaks of a מָדוֹן, a strife, in God's spirit). Ibn Ezra reports two views: 'sheath' (as נָדָן, 1 Chr 21:27, the body being the spirit's sheath), with ידון then from another, hollow root; or from דין, 'judge'. His own sense is 'will not abide' (לֹא יַעֲמֹד). Radak explains the 'sheath' form as a lost nun.
- בְּשַׁגַּם: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take the שַׁ as the relative שֶׁ, with the vowel changed: 'since also'.
- וְהָיוּ is a weqatal: the days 'will be' 120 years, a grant of time.
- The etnaḥta after בָשָׂר divides the verse into the sentence of decision and the term granted.

Note: The English follows Rashi on ידון (contend, quarrel) and לעלם (for a long time), and Rashi and Ibn Ezra on בשגם (since also). The 120 years is read as a respite (Rashi, Sforno, Onkelos), not as the future length of a human life, which Ibn Ezra rejects as untrue. 'My spirit' is God's. The reading 'sheath' and the reading 'judge' are recorded. The lexicon lists a sense under דין for this form; the Qal 6 'contend' is the closest in the list.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'will not quarrel and contend' (יתרעם ויריב): my spirit will not argue with me on account of man.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: לעלם means 'for a long time': my spirit is debating whether to destroy or to have mercy, and this dispute will not last in me for long.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בְּשַׁגַּם is as בְּשֶׁגַּם: 'because this too is in him, that he is flesh, and even so he does not submit before me; what then if he were fire or something hard?' The שַׁ is the relative שֶׁ, as in שַׁקַּמְתִּי (Jgs 5:7) and שָׁאַתָּה (Jgs 6:17).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'until 120 years I will be patient with them; if they do not repent I will bring a flood.' The decree was given twenty years before Noah fathered (the Torah has no earlier and later).
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: some say ידון is like נדן 'sheath', the body being the spirit's sheath (cf. Dan 7:15), and the root is another; others that it is from דין, since the spirit is the body's judge. The English keeps 'contend' from Rashi.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the שׁ is like שֶׁכָּכָה, so 'since also he is flesh': my spirit will not remain, because of the violence, and because man is flesh and reaches his term and fails.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra rejects the view that 120 years is the span of all human life: Shem lived six hundred. He follows the Aramaic translator: God set an end for humankind, as in 'forty days' (Jon 3:4); if they repent they escape. He adds that Scripture has no strict order of events.
- Ramban (records): Ramban rejects Rashi's reading of בשגם and Ibn Ezra's, and takes 'since man is flesh like all flesh, he is not fit to have the spirit of God within him'.
- Radak (records): Radak: ידון is from 'מדון' (strife) by his father, or from 'sheath'; God will extend 120 years if they repent, else destroy.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the שׁ is open like שַׁקַּמְתִּי; 'since he too is flesh'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the days that I will grant him.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: we know only that this was the Creator's will.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: there will be a time for repentance.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: in the meantime Noah was building the ark and warning them.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: לָא יִתְקַיַם דָרָא בִישָׁא הָדֵין קֳדָמַי לְעַלָם ... אַרְכָא יְהִיבַת לְהוֹן מְאָה וְעַשְׂרִין שְׁנִין אִם יְתוּבוּן, 'this evil generation will not stand before me for ever ... a respite of 120 years is given them if they repent'.
- יָדוֹן: 'contend' (Rashi), 'abide', as in a sheath (Ibn Ezra's first), or 'judge' (Ibn Ezra's second); the written form is not otherwise attested.
- The pointing of the divine name is יְהֹוָה (MAM) and is read as 'the LORD'.

Grammar:

- הַנְּפִלִים: Rashi says that in Hebrew the word means 'giants' (עֲנָקִים), and gives a reason for the name: they fell and made the world fall. Ibn Ezra and Radak: the heart of one who sees them falls, astonished at their height.
- יָבֹאוּ is a yiqtol after אֲשֶׁר that, with the weqatal וְיָלְדוּ, expresses repeated action: 'whenever they came ... and bore'.
- הֵמָּה הַגִּבֹּרִים is a verbless clause: the pronoun הֵמָּה ('they') is the subject and הַגִּבֹּרִים the predicate. The darga on הֵמָּה is conjunctive and binds it to the next word; the tevir on הַגִּבֹּרִים is disjunctive.
- מֵעוֹלָם: 'from of old', from long ago; אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם: 'men of the name', men of fame.

Note: הַנְּפִלִים is rendered 'giants': Rashi says this is the word's meaning in Hebrew (לְשׁוֹן עֲנָקִים), Ibn Ezra and Radak explain the name by their height, and the lexicon gives 'giants'; the transliteration 'Nephilim' is given in the token note. וְגַם אַחֲרֵי כֵן: Rashi 'afterward', even though they had seen the destruction of the generation of Enosh; Ibn Ezra 'after the Flood'. The English 'and also afterward' keeps both. הַגִּבֹּרִים are 'warriors' (mighty men); Rashi adds 'to rebel against God'. אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם: Rashi gives two midrashic readings: the men designated by names that speak of destruction (Irad, Mehujael, Methushael), and 'men of desolation' (שִׁמָּמוֹן). The English 'men of renown' follows Radak (they had a name in the mouths of later generations) and Onkelos (אֱנָשִׁין דִּשְׁמָא); Rashi's readings are recorded. The lexicon lists a single sense for the Nephilim entry, which is not a path; the sense is therefore omitted below.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they are called נְפִלִים because they fell and made the world fall; in Hebrew the word means giants (עֲנָקִים). The English follows.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'in those days' means the days of the generation of Enosh and the sons of Cain.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: even though they saw the destruction of the generation of Enosh (the ocean rose and flooded a third of the world), the Flood generation did not learn. The English 'and also afterward' leaves open the event.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they bore giants like themselves.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: הגבורים 'to rebel against the Almighty'. The English keeps the neutral 'warriors'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: אנשי השם are those designated by names that speak of destruction, Irad, Mehujael, Methushael, for they were blotted out (נִמֹּחוּ) and uprooted (הֻתְּשׁוּ); another reading: אַנְשֵׁי שִׁמָּמוֹן, 'men of desolation', who laid the world waste. The English 'men of renown' follows Radak and Onkelos, not Rashi.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: נְפִילִים means that the heart of one who sees them falls, in wonder at their height. The English 'giants' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: אחרי כן means after the Flood; the sons of Anak were from the family of the sons of God.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: Rashi's reason for the name, and the grammarians' (Ibn Ezra, Radak) 'because man's heart falls from fear', cf. האימים (Gn 14:5).
- Ramban (records): Ramban cites Rashi on 'those days', and Ibn Ezra on 'after the Flood', and proposes his own view that the sons of God are Adam, Seth and Enosh and their descendants.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the verse is connected with 'from all that they chose' above.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the Nephilim are the giants, very tall; the name means the viewer falls from astonishment.
- Radak (records): Radak: the Nephilim were sons of the great, and the children begotten by such were like them in quality and quantity.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'who were of old' means they were spoken of by later generations.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'men of the name' means they had a name in the mouths of later generations.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: גִּבָּרַיָּא הֲווֹ בְאַרְעָא בְּיוֹמַיָּא הָאִנּוּן, 'the mighty ones were in the land in those days', rendering נפלים as גבריא; and 'sons of the nobles' for בני האלהים.
- אַחֲרֵי כֵן: after the destruction of Enosh's generation (Rashi) or after the Flood (Ibn Ezra, Ramban's report); kept open.
- The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.

#### Genesis 6:5

> וַיַּ֣רְא יְהֹוָ֔ה כִּ֥י רַבָּ֛ה רָעַ֥ת הָאָדָ֖ם בָּאָ֑רֶץ וְכׇל־יֵ֙צֶר֙ מַחְשְׁבֹ֣ת לִבּ֔וֹ רַ֥ק רַ֖ע כׇּל־הַיּֽוֹם׃

**The LORD saw that the evil of the human was great on the earth, and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day long.**

Literal: and-saw the-LORD that great evil-of the-human in-the-earth and-every formation-of thoughts-of his-heart only evil all-the-day

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |

| יְהֹוָ֔ה | the LORD | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- וַיַּרְא is a wayyiqtol; כִּי introduces the object clause: what the LORD saw.
- רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם: the predicate adjective comes first, and the verb 'to be' is not written. רָעַת is the construct of רָעָה.
- וְכׇל־יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ is a chain of constructs (every / inclination / of thoughts / of his heart) with no verb; רַק רַע is its predicate.
- The etnaḥta on בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the evil on the earth, and then the inward cause.

Note: יֵצֶר is from יצר 'to form, shape'; Radak takes it as the desire of the heart's thinking, which forms and works out matters within the heart. The English 'inclination' follows that. הָאָדָם is 'the human', mankind generally (a collective), per decisions.

Commentary:

- Radak (follows): Radak: of the two inclinations in a person's heart, one good and one bad, here all was bad; the desire of the heart's thought is called יֵצֶר because the heart forms and works things out within itself.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם refers to the past (לְשֶׁעָבַר), and the next clause to the future; this bears on tense reading, not on the English words.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders the verse closely: 'and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day' (יִצְרָא מַחְשְׁבַת לִבֵּהּ לְחוֹד בִּישׁ כָּל יוֹמָא).

#### Genesis 6:6

> וַיִּנָּ֣חֶם יְהֹוָ֔ה כִּֽי־עָשָׂ֥ה אֶת־הָֽאָדָ֖ם בָּאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּתְעַצֵּ֖ב אֶל־לִבּֽוֹ׃

**The LORD regretted that he had made the human on the earth, and was grieved in his heart.**

Literal: and-regretted the-LORD that-made [object-mark] the-human in-the-earth and-grieved-himself to his-heart

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיִּנָּ֣חֶם | and regretted — Niphal wayyiqtol of נחם: 'be sorry, rue' | ו: and + נָחַם | נחם | conjunction + verb (nifal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Niph 2 |
| יְהֹוָ֔ה | the LORD | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |
| כִּֽי | that | כִּי |  | conjunction | 1 |
| עָשָׂ֥ה | he made — perfect, anterior to the regret: 'he had made' | עָשָׂה | עשׂה | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal II.1 |
| אֶת | [object marker] — marks the definite direct object | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| הָֽאָדָ֖ם | the human | ה: the + אָדָם | אדם | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 2 |
| בָּאָ֑רֶץ | on the earth | ב: in, with, by + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | preposition (with definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| וַיִּתְעַצֵּ֖ב | and was grieved — Hithpael wayyiqtol: 'was pained'; the lexicon has only a single Hithp sense | ו: and + עָצַב | עצב | conjunction + verb (hitpael, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hithp |
| אֶל | to | אֶל |  | preposition | 1 |
| לִבּֽוֹ׃ | his heart — construct form with 3rd masculine singular suffix; אֶל־לִבּוֹ 'to/in his heart' | לֵב | לבב | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | II.9 |

Grammar:

- וַיִּנָּחֶם is a Niphal wayyiqtol; the stem is reflexive-passive, 'he let himself be sorry'.
- וַיִּתְעַצֵּב is a Hithpael wayyiqtol, 'he pained himself'; it is the counterpart of the Niphal verb before it.
- אֶל־לִבּוֹ: the phrase is literally 'to his heart', the inward place of thought and feeling.
- The etnaḥta on בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the regret over the making, and then the grief.

Note: The two verbs speak of God in human terms. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban all say the Torah speaks in human language, so the English keeps the verbs plain ('regretted', 'was grieved'). Rashi reads otherwise: first, וַיִּנָּחֶם as consolation (it comforted God that man was made among the lower beings); then, as a change of thought from mercy to judgment, 'he considered what to do'. Both Rashi readings are recorded. בָּאָרֶץ (on the earth) modifies the making: Radak reads it as made of earth.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: נֶחָמָה here is consolation: it was a comfort before God that he had created man among the lower beings, for had he been one of the upper beings he would have led them to rebel. On this reading וַיִּנָּחֶם means 'was consoled', not 'regretted'; the English follows Ibn Ezra's 'regretted' (in human language) and keeps this reading here.
- Rashi (records): Rashi, after Onkelos: 'it arose in the thought of the Place to grieve him' (the object is the human), and another reading: his thought turned from mercy to judgment, as every נִחוּם in Scripture means 'he took counsel what to do'. The English keeps 'regretted' and 'was grieved'; this alternative is kept here.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: he mourned the loss of the work of his hands, as in 'the king was grieved (נֶעֱצַב) over his son'; the narrative of R. Joshua ben Korha shows that God's foreknowledge does not remove the grief.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it is known that God is not a man that he should regret (1 Sam 15:29); the Torah speaks in human language, for one who destroys what he has made appears to feel both (regret and grief).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיִּתְעַצֵּב אֶל לִבּוֹ is the opposite of 'the LORD rejoices in his works' (Ps 104:31); he also rejects the view that 'his heart' means the prophet, for then the text would not say אֶל after the verb.
- Radak (records): Radak: בָּאָרֶץ means man mixed with the products of the earth, whose body is all earthly, unlike the heavenly image of God; this is why God did not regret making Noah.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'the LORD turned in his Memra because he made man on the earth, and said in his Memra to break their strength as his will' (a paraphrase that avoids saying God regretted).

- The two clauses with כִּי form a pair: כִּי נִחַמְתִּי (Niphal) and כִּי עֲשִׂיתִם (Qal), so the regret is tied to the making.
- The etnaḥta on הַשָּׁמָיִם divides the verse: the decree, and then the reason.

Note: The speech is addressed to no one stated. Ibn Ezra's own view is that it is joined to 'his heart' of verse 6 (the speech is inward), and Radak allows 'to Noah'; the English gives the bare 'said'. אֶת־הָאָדָם is 'the human' (mankind), per decisions. 'Whom I created' uses בָּרָא, the verb of Genesis 1, which the lexicon lists as Qal.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: man is dust and God will bring water on him and wipe him out; this is why the verb is of 'wiping' (מִחוּי), which suits that image.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the animals also corrupted their ways (Genesis Rabbah); another reading: everything was made for man, and with him gone what need is there for them. The English gives the plain list and records both reasons.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: כִּי נִחַמְתִּי means 'I have thought what to do about what I made', i.e. נִחוּם as a change of thought. The English keeps the plainer 'I regret'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיֹּאמֶר is said 'to his heart', or to the angels; some say to Noah; the correct view in his eyes is that it is joined to 'his heart' written above. The English leaves the addressee unstated.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: 'the human' and not every person, since Noah and his sons remained; Genesis Rabbah on why water: the human was made only from dust, and only water wipes dust out.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: אֲרֵי תָבִית בְּמֵימְרִי 'for I have turned in my Memra' replaces 'I regret'.

#### Genesis 6:8

> וְנֹ֕חַ מָ֥צָא חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהֹוָֽה׃

**But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.**

Literal: and-Noah found favor in-eyes-of the-LORD

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וְנֹ֕חַ | and Noah — the vav contrasts Noah with the human of the previous verse | ו: and + נֹחַ | נוח | conjunction + noun (proper name) |  |
| מָ֥צָא | found — perfect, 3rd masculine singular, in a clause that begins with the subject | מָצָא | מצא | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| חֵ֖ן | favor — 'favor, acceptance' | חֵן | חנן | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 2 |
| בְּעֵינֵ֥י | in the eyes of — idiom: 'in the eyes of' means 'in the opinion of' | ב: in, with, by + עַ֫יִן | עין | preposition + noun (common, both genders, dual, construct) | 5 |
| יְהֹוָֽה׃ | the LORD | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- וְנֹחַ מָצָא: the subject comes before the verb, so the clause is a contrast with the preceding judgment; hence 'But'.
- מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי is an idiom for 'was acceptable to', literally 'found favor in the eyes of'.
- The zaqef gadol on נֹחַ marks Noah as the subject standing apart, and the silluq closes the paragraph (פ).

Note: The vav is rendered 'But', following the contrast. The lexicon's עַיִן senses list 5 for 'in the presence of', which is the idiom's sense; the sense 2.b etc. are for other uses.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: חֵן is from the root of 'mercy', and so תַּחֲנָה; the sense of 'finding favor' is like 'no eye had pity on you' (Ezekiel 16:5).
- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban: all his deeds were pleasing before God, and this is set against the generation whose deeds caused grief; the next verse then says why.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: Noah's children were saved by favor, not desert, since he did not teach his generation to know God.

## Noach — נֹחַ (Genesis 6:9–11:32)

### Reading text

<sup>6:9</sup> These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generations; Noah walked with God. <sup>6:10</sup> Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. <sup>6:11</sup> The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. <sup>6:12</sup> God saw the earth, and indeed it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.

<sup>6:13</sup> God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is full of violence because of them; now I am about to destroy them with the earth." <sup>6:14</sup> Make yourself an ark of gopher wood; make the ark with compartments, and cover it with pitch inside and out. <sup>6:15</sup> This is how you shall make it: the ark's length shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. <sup>6:16</sup> Make a skylight for the ark, and finish it off to a cubit at the top. Set the door of the ark in its side; make it with lower, second, and third stories. <sup>6:17</sup> As for me, I am about to bring the flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life from under the heavens; everything that is on the earth shall perish. <sup>6:18</sup> I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall enter the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives with you. <sup>6:19</sup> And of every living thing, of all flesh, you shall bring two of each into the ark to keep them alive with you; they shall be male and female. <sup>6:20</sup> Of the birds according to their kind, and of the animals according to their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground according to its kind, two of each will come to you to be kept alive. <sup>6:21</sup> As for you, take for yourself some of every kind of food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself, so that it will be food for you and for them. <sup>6:22</sup> Noah did according to all that God had commanded him; so he did.

<sup>7:1</sup> Then the LORD said to Noah: Come, you and all your household, into the ark, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation. <sup>7:2</sup> Of every clean animal take for yourself seven each, a male and his mate; and of the animals that are not clean, two, a male and his mate. <sup>7:3</sup> Also of the birds of the sky, seven each, male and female, to keep seed alive across the face of all the earth. <sup>7:4</sup> For in seven more days I will make it rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from the face of the ground. <sup>7:5</sup> Noah did according to all that the LORD had commanded him. <sup>7:6</sup> Now Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came, water upon the earth. <sup>7:7</sup> Noah went into the ark, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him, because of the waters of the flood. <sup>7:8</sup> Of the clean animals, and of the animals that are not clean, and of the birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground, <sup>7:9</sup> two by two they came to Noah into the ark, male and female, as God had commanded Noah. <sup>7:10</sup> And when the seven days were over, the waters of the flood were on the earth. <sup>7:11</sup> In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened. <sup>7:12</sup> And the rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights. <sup>7:13</sup> On that very day Noah went in, and Shem and Ham and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and the wife of Noah and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark. <sup>7:14</sup> They and every wild animal according to its kind, and every domestic animal according to its kind, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind, every bird of every kind of wing. <sup>7:15</sup> They came to Noah, into the ark, two by two from all flesh in which there was the breath of life. <sup>7:16</sup> Those that came in, male and female from all flesh, came in as God had commanded him, and the LORD shut him in. <sup>7:17</sup> When the flood had lasted forty days on the earth, the waters increased and lifted the ark, and it rose above the earth. <sup>7:18</sup> The waters grew strong and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark moved on the surface of the waters. <sup>7:19</sup> The waters prevailed very, very greatly on the earth, and all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered. <sup>7:20</sup> Fifteen cubits upward the waters prevailed, and the mountains were covered. <sup>7:21</sup> All flesh that moved on the earth had perished, among birds and livestock and wild animals and among every swarming thing that swarms on the earth, and all humankind. <sup>7:22</sup> Everything that had the breath of the spirit of life in its nostrils, of all that was on dry land, died. <sup>7:23</sup> He wiped out every living thing that was on the surface of the ground, from humans to animals, to crawling things, and to the birds of the sky; they were wiped out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark. <sup>7:24</sup> The waters prevailed over the earth for a hundred and fifty days. <sup>8:1</sup> God remembered Noah and every living creature and all the domestic animals that were with him in the ark, and God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters subsided. <sup>8:2</sup> The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the sky were shut, and the rain from the sky was held back. <sup>8:3</sup> The waters withdrew from the earth steadily, and the waters decreased at the end of a hundred and fifty days. <sup>8:4</sup> The ark came to rest in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on the mountains of Ararat. <sup>8:5</sup> The waters continued to diminish steadily until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains became visible. <sup>8:6</sup> At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made. <sup>8:7</sup> He sent out the raven, and it went back and forth until the waters had dried from off the earth. <sup>8:8</sup> Then he sent the dove away from him, to see whether the waters had abated from the surface of the ground. <sup>8:9</sup> But the dove found no resting place for the sole of her foot, and she returned to him, to the ark, for there was water over the surface of all the earth. So he stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her to him into the ark. <sup>8:10</sup> He waited another seven days, and again he sent the dove away from the ark. <sup>8:11</sup> The dove came to him at evening time, and there in her beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had abated from the earth. <sup>8:12</sup> He waited another seven days and sent the dove away, and she did not return to him any more. <sup>8:13</sup> In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first of the month, the waters dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and there the surface of the ground had dried up. <sup>8:14</sup> In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.

<sup>8:15</sup> Then God spoke to Noah, saying: <sup>8:16</sup> Go out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and your sons' wives with you. <sup>8:17</sup> Bring out with you every living creature that is with you, of all flesh, birds and animals and everything that creeps on the earth, and let them breed abundantly on the earth and be fruitful and multiply on the earth. <sup>8:18</sup> So Noah went out, with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives. <sup>8:19</sup> All the animals, all the creeping things, and all the birds, everything that moves on the earth, went out of the ark by their kinds. <sup>8:20</sup> Then Noah built an altar to the LORD, and he took some of every clean animal and every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. <sup>8:21</sup> The LORD smelled the soothing aroma, and the LORD said to himself, "I will never again curse the ground because of the human, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth; and I will never again strike down every living thing as I have done." <sup>8:22</sup> For as long as the earth lasts, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never cease. <sup>9:1</sup> God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth." <sup>9:2</sup> The fear and dread of you shall be upon every animal of the earth and upon every bird of the sky, upon everything that crawls on the ground and upon all the fish of the sea; into your hand they are given. <sup>9:3</sup> Every moving thing that is alive shall be food for you; as with the green plants, I have given you everything. <sup>9:4</sup> Only flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat. <sup>9:5</sup> But your blood, for your lives, I will demand; from every animal I will demand it, and from the human, from each man for his brother, I will demand the life of the human. <sup>9:6</sup> Whoever sheds the blood of the human, by the human his blood shall be shed; for in the image of God He made the human. <sup>9:7</sup> As for you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm over the earth and multiply in it.

<sup>9:8</sup> Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him: <sup>9:9</sup> As for me, I am establishing my covenant with you and with your offspring after you, <sup>9:10</sup> and with every living creature that is with you, among the birds, among the livestock, and among every animal of the earth that is with you, from all that came out of the ark, to every animal of the earth. <sup>9:11</sup> I will establish my covenant with you: never again will any flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth. <sup>9:12</sup> Then God said: This is the sign of the covenant that I am giving between me and you and between every living creature that is with you, for everlasting generations. <sup>9:13</sup> I have now set my bow in the cloud, and it will become a sign of a covenant between me and the earth. <sup>9:14</sup> When I bring clouds over the earth, the bow will appear in the cloud. <sup>9:15</sup> I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and between every living creature among all flesh, and never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all flesh. <sup>9:16</sup> The bow will be in the cloud, and I will see it, to remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living being, among all flesh that is on the earth. <sup>9:17</sup> God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."

<sup>9:18</sup> The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham was the father of Canaan. <sup>9:19</sup> These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the whole earth was dispersed. <sup>9:20</sup> Noah, a man of the soil, began and planted a vineyard. <sup>9:21</sup> He drank some of the wine, became drunk, and uncovered himself inside his tent. <sup>9:22</sup> Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside. <sup>9:23</sup> Shem and Japheth took the garment and laid it on both their shoulders, and they walked backward and covered their father's nakedness, and their faces were backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness. <sup>9:24</sup> Noah woke from his wine and learned what his youngest son had done to him. <sup>9:25</sup> He said, "Cursed be Canaan; a slave among slaves shall he be to his brothers." <sup>9:26</sup> He said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem, and may Canaan be a slave to them." <sup>9:27</sup> May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem; and may Canaan be a slave to them. <sup>9:28</sup> After the flood Noah lived three hundred and fifty years. <sup>9:29</sup> All the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.

<sup>10:1</sup> These are the descendants of Noah's sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth: children were born to them after the flood. <sup>10:2</sup> The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. <sup>10:3</sup> The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. <sup>10:4</sup> The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. <sup>10:5</sup> From these the coastlands of the nations were separated in their lands, each according to its language, by their clans, in their nations. <sup>10:6</sup> The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. <sup>10:7</sup> The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. <sup>10:8</sup> Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be a mighty man on the earth. <sup>10:9</sup> He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; therefore it is said, Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD. <sup>10:10</sup> The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Akkad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. <sup>10:11</sup> From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah, <sup>10:12</sup> and Resen, between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city. <sup>10:13</sup> And Egypt fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim, <sup>10:14</sup> the Pathrusim, the Casluhim, from whom the Philistines came, and the Caphtorim.

<sup>10:15</sup> Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth. <sup>10:16</sup> the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites. <sup>10:17</sup> the Hivites, the Arkites, and the Sinites. <sup>10:18</sup> the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites spread out. <sup>10:19</sup> The border of the Canaanites ran from Sidon toward Gerar, as far as Gaza; toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. <sup>10:20</sup> These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, in their nations.

<sup>10:21</sup> Children were born to Shem also, the father of all the sons of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder. <sup>10:22</sup> The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram. <sup>10:23</sup> The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash. <sup>10:24</sup> Arphaxad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber. <sup>10:25</sup> To Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and the name of his brother was Joktan. <sup>10:26</sup> Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, <sup>10:27</sup> Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, <sup>10:28</sup> Obal, Abimael, Sheba, <sup>10:29</sup> Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan. <sup>10:30</sup> Their homeland stretched from Mesha, as you go toward Sephar, to the eastern mountain. <sup>10:31</sup> These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, by their nations. <sup>10:32</sup> These are the clans of the sons of Noah, by their lineages, in their nations; and from these the nations were divided on the earth after the flood.

<sup>11:1</sup> Now the whole earth had one language and the same words. <sup>11:2</sup> As they traveled from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. <sup>11:3</sup> They said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and burn them hard." So brick served them as stone, and bitumen served them as mortar. <sup>11:4</sup> Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered over the face of the whole earth." <sup>11:5</sup> The LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the children of the human were building. <sup>11:6</sup> The LORD said, "Look, they are one people with one language for all of them, and this is what they have begun to do. Now nothing will be held back from them that they plan to do." <sup>11:7</sup> "Come, let us go down and confuse their language there, so that they will not understand one another's language." <sup>11:8</sup> So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they stopped building the city. <sup>11:9</sup> Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth; and from there the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.

<sup>11:10</sup> These are the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arpachshad, two years after the flood. <sup>11:11</sup> And Shem lived, after he fathered Arpachshad, five hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:12</sup> Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and fathered Shelah. <sup>11:13</sup> Arpachshad lived, after he fathered Shelah, four hundred and three years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:14</sup> Shelah lived thirty years, and he fathered Eber. <sup>11:15</sup> Shelah lived four hundred and three years after fathering Eber, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:16</sup> Eber lived thirty-four years, and he fathered Peleg. <sup>11:17</sup> Eber lived four hundred and thirty years after fathering Peleg, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:18</sup> Peleg lived thirty years, and he fathered Reu. <sup>11:19</sup> After he fathered Reu, Peleg lived two hundred nine years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:20</sup> Reu lived thirty-two years, and he fathered Serug. <sup>11:21</sup> After he fathered Serug, Reu lived two hundred seven years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:22</sup> Serug lived thirty years, and he fathered Nahor. <sup>11:23</sup> Serug lived, after he fathered Nahor, two hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:24</sup> Nahor lived twenty-nine years, and he fathered Terah. <sup>11:25</sup> Nahor lived, after he fathered Terah, one hundred nineteen years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

<sup>11:26</sup> Terah lived seventy years, and he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran. <sup>11:27</sup> These are the generations of Terah: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot. <sup>11:28</sup> Haran died in the lifetime of his father Terah, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans. <sup>11:29</sup> Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. <sup>11:30</sup> Sarai was barren; she had no child. <sup>11:31</sup> Terah took his son Abram, and Lot, the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram, and they went out with them from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan; they came as far as Haran and settled there. <sup>11:32</sup> The days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.

### Noach by verse

#### Genesis 6:9

> אֵ֚לֶּה תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת נֹ֔חַ נֹ֗חַ אִ֥ישׁ צַדִּ֛יק תָּמִ֥ים הָיָ֖ה בְּדֹֽרֹתָ֑יו אֶת־הָֽאֱלֹהִ֖ים הִֽתְהַלֶּךְ־נֹֽחַ׃

**These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generations; Noah walked with God.**

Literal: these generations-of Noah Noah man righteous blameless was in-generations-his with-the-God walked-habitually Noah

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| אֵ֚לֶּה | these | אֵ֫לֶּה | אלה | pronoun (demonstrative, common, plural) | b |
| תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת | generations of, the account of — construct plural; the word introduces an account of Noah and what came of him | תּוֹלֵדוֹת | ילד | noun (common, feminine, plural, construct) |  |
| נֹ֔חַ | Noah | נֹחַ | נוח | noun (proper name) |  |
| נֹ֗חַ | Noah — repeated name, with revia: the account is interrupted and Noah is named again as the subject of the new clause | נֹחַ | נוח | noun (proper name) |  |
| אִ֥ישׁ | a man | אִישׁ | אישׁ | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| צַדִּ֛יק | righteous | צַדִּיק | צדק | adjective (adjective, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| תָּמִ֥ים | blameless | תָּמִים | תמם | adjective (adjective, masculine, singular, absolute) | 4 |
| הָיָ֖ה | was — qal qatal of הָיָה, 'was'; the predicate אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים stands before it | הָיָה | היה | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III |
| בְּדֹֽרֹתָ֑יו | in his generations — plural of דּוֹר with the 3rd masculine singular suffix, written defectively (no vav in either syllable); 'his generations' are the people of his lifetime, which Ibn Ezra extends to the generations after the flood | ב: in, with, by + דּוֹר | דור | preposition + noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 2 |
| אֶת | with — אֵת here is the preposition 'with', not the object marker, after הִתְהַלֵּךְ | אֵת |  | preposition | 1 |
| הָֽאֱלֹהִ֖ים | the God — אֱלֹהִים with the article, the one true God | ה: the + אֱלֹהִים | אלה | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| הִֽתְהַלֶּךְ | walked — hitpael qatal: habitual walking back and forth; Rashi says the form is simply past | הָלַךְ | הלך | verb (hitpael, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hithp |
| נֹֽחַ׃ | Noah — subject placed after the verb; silluq closes the verse | נֹחַ | נוח | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- תּוֹלְדֹת is in the construct state, bound to נֹחַ; the account that follows begins not with Noah's sons but with his praise (so Rashi: הוֹאִיל וְהִזְכִּירוֹ סִפֵּר בְּשִׁבְחוֹ).
- The zaqef qaton on the first נֹחַ closes the heading אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ; the repeated נֹחַ, which carries the revia, begins a new clause as its subject: 'Noah was a righteous man'.
- אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים: the two adjectives stand side by side, each describing 'man'; this predicate is placed before the verb הָיָה.
- הִתְהַלֶּךְ is a hitpael perfect with no vav; Rashi notes that in this stem the same form serves for the future (imperative) and the past, here the past.
- The etnaḥta on בְּדֹרֹתָיו divides the verse: the first half describes Noah, the second his relation to God.

Note: 'Generations' for תּוֹלְדֹת keeps the word's range (descendants, history, account); Ibn Ezra reads it as 'events', Ramban as the plain sense 'descendants'. The phrase בְּדֹרֹתָיו is left as 'in his generations', which keeps both readings (in his own age, and in the ages after the flood) and the disputed praise/blame reading of Rashi's rabbis. 'With God' for אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים follows the preposition אֵת; the old 'walked before' of Abraham is a different construction.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: since the text mentions Noah, it goes on to praise him, as 'the memory of the righteous is for a blessing'; or it teaches that the true generations (offspring) of the righteous are their good deeds. The English keeps 'generations', which allows this.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: some of our rabbis read בְּדֹרֹתָיו as praise (he would have been more righteous in a righteous generation) and some as disparagement (righteous only relative to his generation; beside Abraham he would count for nothing). The English leaves the phrase as 'in his generations' and does not decide between them.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: of Abraham it says 'before whom I walked', but Noah needed support to hold him up, while Abraham strengthened himself and walked in his righteousness on his own. The English 'walked with God' keeps the preposition אֵת; the contrast with Abraham is in the commentary.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: הִתְהַלֵּךְ is past in meaning; in the pattern of this stem the same form serves for the future and the past, as with קוּם הִתְהַלֵּךְ (future) against הִתְהַלֶּךְ נֹחַ (past). The English uses the past tense.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: תּוֹלְדֹת means 'events', as in מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם and אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת יַעֲקֹב. The English 'generations' does not exclude it, and the note records it. Ramban rejects this and keeps 'descendants'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on אִישׁ צַדִּיק: 'in his deeds'. Righteous is read as righteous in conduct, which is the plain English.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: תָּמִים is 'in his heart', as צַדִּיק is 'in his deeds' (6:9:2). Grammatically תָּמִים is an adjective (תֹּאַר הַשֵּׁם) from the geminate verbs (פַּעֲלֵי הַכֶּפֶל), root תמם. The English 'blameless' is read as sound and whole, so the pair means righteous in act, whole in heart.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בְּדֹרֹתָיו means in his generation at the time of the flood and in the generations after, for Noah lived until Abraham was fifty-eight. The plural 'in his generations' in the English admits this reading.

Apparatus:

- Rashi's two rabbinic readings of בְּדֹרֹתָיו (praise or blame, b. Sanhedrin 108a) are both left open.
- אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים: אֵת is read as the preposition 'with' (cf. Rashi's comparison with Abraham's 'before whom'); the pack gives the lemma as the preposition for this token.

#### Genesis 6:10

> וַיּ֥וֹלֶד נֹ֖חַ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה בָנִ֑ים אֶת־שֵׁ֖ם אֶת־חָ֥ם וְאֶת־יָֽפֶת׃

**Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.**

Literal: and-fathered Noah three sons ACC-Shem ACC-Ham and-ACC-Japheth

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיּ֥וֹלֶד | and fathered — hifil wayyiqtol of יָלַד: 'beget, father' | ו: and + יָלַד | ילד | conjunction + verb (hifil, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 1 |
| נֹ֖חַ | Noah | נֹחַ | נוח | noun (proper name) |  |
| שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה | three — masculine cardinal, here before its noun | שָׁלֹשׁ | שׁלשׁ | adjective (cardinal number, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| בָנִ֑ים | sons | בֵּן |  | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 1 |
| אֶת | (object marker) — marks the following name as a direct object, in apposition to 'three sons' | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| שֵׁ֖ם | Shem | שֵׁם |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| אֶת | (object marker) | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| חָ֥ם | Ham | חָם |  | noun (proper name) | 1 |
| וְאֶת | and (object marker) — the vav joins the last item of the list | ו: and + אֵת | אות | conjunction + particle (direct object marker) |  |
| יָֽפֶת׃ | Japheth | יֶ֫פֶת |  | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- וַיּוֹלֶד is hifil wayyiqtol of יָלַד; the hifil is the usual form for a father's begetting.
- שְׁלֹשָׁה has the ending ־ָה yet goes with the masculine בָּנִים: from three to ten, the cardinal takes in form the opposite gender to its noun.
- The three names are each marked with אֶת, in apposition to שְׁלֹשָׁה בָנִים.
- The etnaḥta on בָנִים separates the number from the list of names.

Note: The verse repeats what 5:32 already said; the commentators (Radak, Ramban, Sforno) explain why, but the English simply states it. In this unit the lexicon gives the lemma of שֵׁם as 'Sem'; the English form is Shem, following the decisions.

Commentary:

- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban: Japheth is the eldest (10:21 אֲחִי יֶפֶת הַגָּדוֹל; his sons are listed first in chapter 10) and Ham the youngest (9:24 בְּנוֹ הַקָּטָן). Shem is put first for his eminence, Ham follows him in birth order, and so Japheth comes last; the verse does not say 'Shem, Japheth and Ham', which would set all three out of birth order. The English keeps the Hebrew order, so the comment does not change it.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the sons were already named above (5:32); they are named again here, right after 'Noah walked with God', to teach that as he devoted himself to serving God, so he taught and trained his sons to turn from the ways of the wicked and to serve the LORD. Had they not been so, they would not have been saved, for Ezekiel 14 says that Noah, Daniel and Job would save neither sons nor daughters; through them seed remained after the flood.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'And Noah fathered three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth', the same plain sense.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: from the time he began to rebuke his generation, he earned sons; a homiletical reading that does not bear on the English.

#### Genesis 6:11

> וַתִּשָּׁחֵ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ לִפְנֵ֣י הָֽאֱלֹהִ֑ים וַתִּמָּלֵ֥א הָאָ֖רֶץ חָמָֽס׃

**The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.**

Literal: and-was-corrupted the-earth before the-God and-was-filled the-earth violence

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַתִּשָּׁחֵ֥ת | and was corrupted — nifal wayyiqtol, feminine, because הָאָרֶץ is feminine here | ו: and + שָׁחַת | שׁחת | conjunction + verb (nifal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Niph |
| הָאָ֖רֶץ | the earth — a metonymy: the earth for the people of the earth (Ibn Ezra, Radak) | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.c |
| לִפְנֵ֣י | before — לִפְנֵי: literally 'to the face of' | ל: to, for + פָּנֶה | פנה | preposition + noun (common, both genders, plural, construct) | I.6 |
| הָֽאֱלֹהִ֑ים | God — with the article, the one true God | ה: the + אֱלֹהִים | אלה | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| וַתִּמָּלֵ֥א | and was filled — nifal wayyiqtol, feminine singular | ו: and + מָלֵא | מלא | conjunction + verb (nifal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Niph 1 |
| הָאָ֖רֶץ | the earth | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| חָמָֽס׃ | with violence — an accusative of material after a verb of filling, without a preposition | חָמָס | חמס | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- The two verbs are nifal wayyiqtol, both 3rd feminine singular, to agree with הָאָרֶץ.
- וַתִּשָּׁחֵת and וַתִּמָּלֵא are parallel: the first says the earth was corrupted, the second what filled it.
- חָמָס follows וַתִּמָּלֵא directly, with no preposition: a verb of filling keeps the thing that fills as an accusative even in the nifal, and English supplies 'with'.
- The etnaḥta on הָאֱלֹהִים divides the verse into two parallel halves, each with the earth as subject.
- שָׁחַת and its related forms recur in the next verse (נִשְׁחָתָה, הִשְׁחִית) and make a play on the one root.

Note: 'Earth' is kept for הָאָרֶץ; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the people of the earth (BDB 1.c, 'earth = inhabitants of earth'), and the English leaves the metonymy for the reader. 'Was corrupt' gives the nifal of שָׁחַת, 'be spoiled, ruined'; Rashi specifies the corruption as sexual immorality and idolatry, which 'corrupt' allows. 'Violence' for חָמָס covers Rashi's robbery and Ibn Ezra's robbery, oppression and seizing women by force.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַתִּשָּׁחֵת is the language of sexual immorality and idolatry, as in 'lest you corrupt yourselves'. The English 'corrupt' covers both.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi on חָמָס: robbery (גֶּזֶל). The English 'violence' is the word that includes robbery.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'the earth' means the people of the earth, as in 'when a land sins against me' and 'all the earth came to Egypt'. The English keeps 'earth' as a metonymy for them.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: חָמָס is robbery, oppression and taking women by force. The English 'violence' covers these.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'the people of the earth', as in 'and the land was filled with them' (Exod. 1:7).
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים tells us that God watches over the lower world. It is a theological gloss and does not change the English.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak on וַתִּמָּלֵא: God saw and decided to wipe it out, as 'before God' implies; a comment on the narrative, not on the wording.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: the earth was corrupted before the LORD and filled with robberies (חֲטוֹפִין): the same plain sense, with 'robbery' for חָמָס.

Apparatus:

- לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים: 'before God' as 'in God's sight' or 'in God's presence'; Ibn Ezra's note at 6:11:2 (given under 6:12) discusses the two readings.

#### Genesis 6:12

> וַיַּ֧רְא אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הָאָ֖רֶץ וְהִנֵּ֣ה נִשְׁחָ֑תָה כִּֽי־הִשְׁחִ֧ית כׇּל־בָּשָׂ֛ר אֶת־דַּרְכּ֖וֹ עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

**God saw the earth, and indeed it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.**

Literal: and-saw God ACC-the-earth and-behold was-corrupted for corrupted all flesh ACC way-its upon the-earth

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיַּ֧רְא | and saw | ו: and + רָאָה | ראה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1.b |
| אֱלֹהִ֛ים | God — without the article, as the subject: God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 4 |
| אֶת | (object marker) — marks 'the earth' as the direct object | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| הָאָ֖רֶץ | the earth | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| וְהִנֵּ֣ה | and behold, and indeed — וְהִנֵּה draws attention to what is seen | ו: and + הִנֵּה |  | conjunction + particle (demonstrative) |  |
| נִשְׁחָ֑תָה | it was corrupted — nifal qatal, feminine singular, with the sense of a state: 'was corrupt'; the nifal can be read as passive or as state | שָׁחַת | שׁחת | verb (nifal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Niph |
| כִּֽי | for — כִּי gives the reason, 'for, because' | כִּי |  | conjunction | 3 |
| הִשְׁחִ֧ית | had corrupted — hifil qatal of the same root; the active, causative counterpart of נִשְׁחָתָה, and a pluperfect in sense | שָׁחַת | שׁחת | verb (hifil, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 2 |
| כׇּל | all | כֹּל | כלל | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 1 |
| בָּשָׂ֛ר | flesh — 'all flesh' is a standard phrase for all living creatures; the commentators dispute whether it means only humans | בָּשָׂר | בשׂר | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 2 |
| אֶת | (object marker) — marks 'its way' as the direct object | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| דַּרְכּ֖וֹ | its way — construct with suffix, 'his way'; the pronoun refers back to 'flesh' | דֶּ֫רֶךְ | דרך | noun (common, both genders, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 4 |
| עַל | on | עַל | עלה | preposition | II.1 |
| הָאָֽרֶץ׃ | the earth | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |

Grammar:

- וְהִנֵּה marks what God sees, from the point of view of the one who sees: 'and there, it was corrupt'.
- נִשְׁחָתָה (nifal, 'was corrupted') and הִשְׁחִית (hifil, 'corrupted') are the same root in two stems: the earth is ruined because all flesh ruined its way.
- כׇּל־בָּשָׂר, 'all flesh', can mean every living creature or all humankind; here Rashi and Ibn Ezra include the animals, while Ramban and Radak take it by the plain sense as humankind.
- The suffix in דַּרְכּוֹ is singular, referring back to 'flesh' taken as a whole.
- The etnaḥta on נִשְׁחָתָה divides the seeing from the reason.

Note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that 'all flesh' here includes the animals (beasts and birds mating with kinds not their own), and that 'its way' is the natural way of begetting: Ibn Ezra endorses the ancients' כָּל חַי לֹא שָׁמַר דֶּרֶךְ תּוֹלַדְתּוֹ. The English 'all flesh had corrupted its way' carries this reading without narrowing it. Ramban, by the plain sense, and Radak take 'all flesh' as humankind, and Onkelos adds אֱנַשׁ. The hifil הִשְׁחִית is taken as a pluperfect ('had corrupted') because it gives the cause of the state just described (נִשְׁחָתָה).

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi on כִּי הִשְׁחִית כׇּל בָּשָׂר: even beasts, wild animals and birds joined with kinds not their own. The English 'all flesh' does not exclude animals, so this is kept open.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (6:11): some say it means 'openly'; others say they corrupted themselves in secret, in hidden matters known only to God. The nearest reading in his view is that the Torah speaks in human language so that the hearers understand: like a servant who commits a transgression in front of his master and does not fear him. Those who say that אֱלֹהִים here is not holy (that is, means judges or rulers) have said nothing. The English 'before God' fits his reading.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: what our ancients said, that הִשְׁחִית כָּל בָּשָׂר אֶת דַּרְכּוֹ means every living creature failed to keep the way of its generation and twisted the known, planted path, is correct (נָכוֹן הוּא); he also praises the homily that they corrupted themselves with 'water' and God judged them with water, from above and below. With Rashi, he takes 'all flesh' to include the animals and 'its way' as the natural way of begetting; the English 'all flesh had corrupted its way' carries that reading.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: if 'all flesh' is taken literally, with Rashi (beasts, animals and birds mating with other kinds), then 'filled with violence because of them' (6:13) means because of some of them, and only man's punishment is told; or the animals too broke their nature, every beast preying and every bird tearing, so that they also did violence. But by the plain sense כָּל בָּשָׂר here is all humankind, as in Isa 66:23, while below (6:19, 7:15) it means every living body. The English keeps the wider 'all flesh'.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: only the opening word וּפֵרוּשׁ ('and its meaning'); the explanation follows in radak:6:12:2.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'all flesh' means human beings, as in 'let all flesh bless' (Ps 145:21) and 'all flesh shall come' (Isa 66:23); but by the words of our rabbis the other living creatures are included as well, as he wrote earlier. The English does not narrow 'all flesh' to people.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'its way' is the way of its begetting, like 'and he shall cleave to his wife'. The English leaves 'way' open.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: 'And the LORD saw the earth, and it was corrupted, for all flesh, man, had corrupted its way': אֱנַשׁ glosses כָּל בָּשָׂר as humans, which is a narrower reading than the English.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno on וְהִנֵּה נִשְׁחָתָה: it was corrupt of itself, with no punishment having come; it describes the cause and does not change the wording.

Apparatus:

- Subject of 6:12.1: אֱלֹהִים without the article, 'God'; Onkelos renders it יְיָ, 'the LORD'.
- 'All flesh' including the animals (Rashi; Ibn Ezra, endorsing the ancients) or all humankind (Ramban by the plain sense, Radak, Onkelos with אֱנַשׁ): the English keeps the wider phrase.

#### Genesis 6:13

> וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֜ים לְנֹ֗חַ קֵ֤ץ כׇּל־בָּשָׂר֙ בָּ֣א לְפָנַ֔י כִּֽי־מָלְאָ֥ה הָאָ֛רֶץ חָמָ֖ס מִפְּנֵיהֶ֑ם וְהִנְנִ֥י מַשְׁחִיתָ֖ם אֶת־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

**God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is full of violence because of them; now I am about to destroy them with the earth."**

Literal: and-said God to-Noah end-of all-of flesh has-come to-before-me for has-been-full the-earth violence from-before-them and-behold-I destroying-them [with/from] the-earth

| אֱלֹהִ֜ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| לְנֹ֗חַ | to Noah | ל: to, for + נֹחַ | נוח | preposition + noun (proper name) |  |

| כִּֽי | for | כִּי |  | conjunction | 3 |

| חָמָ֖ס | violence | חָמָס | חמס | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- קֵץ כׇּל־בָּשָׂר is a construct chain: 'the end of all flesh'; the pashta on בָּשָׂר closes the subject.
- The perfect בָּא ('has come') and מָלְאָה ('is full') state the present result of what has happened.
- וְהִנְנִי with the participle מַשְׁחִיתָם is the idiom of imminent action: 'and behold I am about to destroy'.
- אֶת־הָאָרֶץ: אֶת is the usual object marker, but the commentators read it as 'from' or 'with' because the object of מַשְׁחִית is already -ם.
- The etnaḥta on מִפְּנֵיהֶם divides the verse: reason for the decree, then the decree itself.

Note: אֶת־הָאָרֶץ: Rashi first reads אֶת as 'from the earth' (like כְּצֵאתִי אֶת הָעִיר), and then, as a second explanation, as 'with the earth', so that the earth too is ruined. Ibn Ezra lists 'from' and 'with' but prefers that מַשְׁחִיתָם does double duty: 'I am destroying them and destroying the earth'. The English takes 'with', the reading the two share; the other readings are recorded. The pack's parse gives אֶת as a preposition, which agrees. חָמָס is the word on which Rashi (Sanhedrin 108) says the decree was sealed.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: wherever one finds sexual immorality and idolatry, a destroying force (androlomusia) comes into the world and kills good and wicked alike. A homily on 'the end of all flesh'; it does not change the plain sense.
- Rashi (records): Rashi, citing Sanhedrin 108: their sentence was sealed only on account of robbery (גָּזֵל). He reads חָמָס here as robbery. The English keeps BDB's broader 'violence', which includes it, and records Rashi's narrower sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: אֶת means 'from the earth', like כְּצֵאתִי אֶת הָעִיר and חָלָה אֶת רַגְלָיו; another explanation: 'with the earth', since even three handbreadths of plowed depth were dissolved. The English adopts the second explanation, 'with'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בָּשָׂר means 'the body' (הוּא הַגּוּף). The English 'flesh' is used for the living creature as a bodily being.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בָּא means 'arrived': the end of their calamity (הִגִּיעַ קֵץ אֵידָם) has arrived. The English 'has come' is the same.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: אֶת is 'from the earth' or 'with', like אֶת יַעֲקֹב אִישׁ וּבֵיתוֹ, but he prefers that מַשְׁחִיתָם serves two objects: 'I am destroying them, and destroying the earth'. The English follows the 'with' option; his preferred construction is recorded.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra's preferred reading: 'I am about to destroy them and to destroy the earth' (מַשְׁחִית has a second, implied object).
- Rashi's first reading of אֶת: 'from the earth', that is, I will destroy them out of the earth.
- The Targum Onkelos renders 'with the earth' (עִם אַרְעָא), agreeing with 'with'.

Grammar:

- The two verbs עֲשֵׂה (imperative) and תַּעֲשֶׂה (imperfect) repeat 'make', the second adding what the ark is to have.
- קִנִּים is placed first for emphasis; it is the object of the idea 'make the ark with nests'.
- וְכָפַרְתָּ is a denominative verb built on כֹּפֶר 'pitch', with the cognate noun after it (figura etymologica): 'pitch it with pitch'.
- מִבַּיִת וּמִחוּץ: 'from the inside and from the outside', an idiom for 'inside and out'.
- The etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה separates the building from the sealing.

Note: גֹּפֶר is a hapax and the species is not known; the English keeps the Hebrew word. Rashi connects it with גָּפְרִית 'brimstone'; Ibn Ezra says only that it is a light wood that floats. קִנִּים is 'nests' and so 'compartments' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak). כֹּפֶר is 'pitch' (Rashi: Aramaic זפת; BDB agrees).

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: God had many ways to save Noah, but made him build so that the people would see him at work for 120 years and ask, and he would tell them of the coming flood, so that they might repent. A homily on motive.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'gopher' is its name; and why this kind? On account of the brimstone (גָּפְרִית) by which they were doomed. The English keeps the name 'gopher'; the explanation is not needed for the plain sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: קִנִּים are 'dwellings' (מְדוֹרִים), separate quarters for each beast and animal. The English 'compartments'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: כֹּפֶר is pitch (זֶפֶת) in Aramaic; the Talmud has כּוּפְרָא; here he coated it inside and out because of the strength of the water. The English 'pitch'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: גֹּפֶר is the name of a wood that is light on water, with no parallel in Scripture. The English keeps 'gopher'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: קִנִּים means that every beast, bird and animal, a male and his mate, will be alone in its own place. The English 'compartments'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it says תֵּבָה and not a ship, since it has not the form of a ship and has no oars. The English 'ark'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra gives several views. Some derive וְכָפַרְתָּ from כַּפֹּרֶת ('cover'), meaning a smeared-on covering. Some say כֹּפֶר is something like pitch, some a sticky clay from the ground that holds like pitch, and some the substance named in Arabic with qof for kaf. He holds that וְכָפַרְתָּ comes from the noun בַּכֹּפֶר, 'pitch it with pitch'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מִבַּיִת is like לְפָנִים, 'within'. The English 'inside'.

Apparatus:

- Rashi: כֹּפֶר is pitch (זֶפֶת) in Aramaic, the Talmud's כּוּפְרָא. Moses' basket (Exodus 2:3) sat in calm water, so clay inside and pitch outside was enough, and the righteous child was spared the smell of pitch. Here, because of the force of the water, the ark was pitched inside and out.
- Onkelos: 'of kedrom wood' (קַדְרוֹם), a cedar kind, per Radak.
- Radak: the outer coat may fail under the force of the water, while the inner holds.

Note: The cubit is the unit of the Torah; the commentators give no other reading of the numbers.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the sense is 'this is the measure that you shall make'; its height is a tenth of its length, so that it floats on the water and the wind does not overturn it. The English 'this is how you shall make it'.

Apparatus:

- Radak (from Bereshit Rabbah): the width is a sixth and the height a tenth of the length, so that it stays level on the water.
- Onkelos agrees: 'this is what you shall make it'.

- The adjectives תַּחְתִּיִּם שְׁנִיִּם וּשְׁלִשִׁים are used as nouns for the three storeys: 'lower, second, third'.
- The tevir on תַּחְתִּיִּם and the tipḥa on וּשְׁלִשִׁים divide the three storeys from the verb.

The English keeps the sense 'finish off the top to a cubit'. The pack notes that the WLC reads תְּכַלֶנָּה, without the dagesh.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: some say a window and some a precious stone that gave them light. The English 'skylight' follows the first and records the second.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: its roof was sloping and rose until it was narrow at the top, standing on one cubit, so that the water runs off on both sides. The English 'finish it off to a cubit at the top'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: set the door in the side so that the rains would not fall into it. The English 'in its side'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: three decks, one above another: the upper for people, the middle for dwelling, the lower for waste. The English 'lower, second, and third stories'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: צֹהַר is a place by which light enters, from צָהֳרַיִם, made at the top; the ark is like a triangle with a sharp top, so that it does not turn over; the door is in one side and reached by a ladder. The English 'skylight'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: תַּחְתִּיִּם is an adjective of the noun, and so שְׁנִיִּם and שְׁלִשִׁים; he answers those who ask why the text does not say שְׁלִישִׁיִּים. The English reads the three words as 'lower, second and third'.

Apparatus:

- צֹהַר: roof (BDB), window (Rashi, Radak), a gem (Rashi, Radak), an opening for light (Ibn Ezra).
- Rashi: וְאֶל־אַמָּה is the roof narrowing to a cubit. Ibn Ezra: the ark is a triangle in section, with its top a cubit long.
- Radak on תַּחְתִּיִּים: the yod is the yod of relation, and the yod of the plural has been dropped, like עֲבָדִים נָכְרִים.
- Sforno: תַּחְתִּיִּם שְׁנִיִּם וּשְׁלִשִׁים means those that are used to ships (הַמּוּרְגָּלִים בָּאֳנִיּוֹת), that is, ships' decks.
- תְּכַלֶּ֣נָּה: WLC reads תְּכַלֶ֣נָּה (vowels)

Note: וַאֲנִי: Rashi hears God agreeing with those who urged him (Psalm 8:5); Ramban reads 'I also', as in וְיִסַּרְתִּי אֶתְכֶם אַף אָנִי. The English keeps the emphasis ('As for me') without choosing. מַבּוּל is the word for the flood; Rashi and Ibn Ezra give derivations (from בלל, בלה, נבל) but the sense is 'flood'. Radak (6:17:4) says כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ means on dry land, not fish.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'I am ready to agree with those who urged me and said, What is man that You remember him (Ps 8)'. A homily on the emphatic וַאֲנִי; it does not alter the plain sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: מַבּוּל is from the sense of destroying (בִּלָּה), confusing (בִּלְבֵּל), or carrying (הוֹבִיל) all from the high to the low; Onkelos renders טוֹפָנָא, flooding everything. The English 'the flood'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the dagesh in the bet of מַבּוּל stands for an assimilated nun, as in מַבּוּעַ, from אָבְלָה נָבְלָה הָאָרֶץ; others derive it from בְּלוּלָה בַּשֶּׁמֶן. The English 'flood'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַמַּבּוּל מַיִם is a short way of saying 'the flood, a flood of waters', as in לְמִן הַיּוֹם הִוָּסְדָה. The English 'the flood of waters'.

Apparatus:

- Ramban on וַאֲנִי: 'I too', as in וְיִסַּרְתִּי אֶתְכֶם אַף אָנִי; the flood is God's own act against those who ruined the earth.
- Radak on הַמַּבּוּל מַיִם: the construct is understood (מַבּוּל מַיִם), and מַבּוּל is a descriptive name for whatever falls from heaven.
- Radak on כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ: on dry land; fish are not included (the creatures of the sea did not share the wicked way, on the view of the Sages).

#### Genesis 6:18

> וַהֲקִמֹתִ֥י אֶת־בְּרִיתִ֖י אִתָּ֑ךְ וּבָאתָ֙ אֶל־הַתֵּבָ֔ה אַתָּ֕ה וּבָנֶ֛יךָ וְאִשְׁתְּךָ֥ וּנְשֵֽׁי־בָנֶ֖יךָ אִתָּֽךְ׃

**I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall enter the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives with you.**

Grammar:

- וַהֲקִמֹתִי is a weqatal verb continuing the speech; the vav is not 'and' in the English, and the verb is future.
- The suffix of אִתָּךְ is written with a final ךְ and a qamets: this is the pausal form of 'with you' (masculine) before the etnaḥta and silluq.
- הֲקִמֹתִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי: the hifil of קוּם takes בְּרִית with the sense of 'confirm, carry out' a covenant.
- The list אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ וְאִשְׁתְּךָ וּנְשֵׁי־בָנֶיךָ names the eight persons: men before women, as the commentators note.
- The zaqef gadol on אַתָּה begins the list of those who enter.

Note: הֲקִמֹתִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי: the first mention of בְּרִית in the Torah. Ibn Ezra first explains it as God's oath that Noah and his sons would not die in the flood, then says the view nearest his own is that the covenant alludes to the rainbow. Ramban takes the plain sense as a covenant of survival (the commitment to bring them safely through). The English keeps 'covenant' without deciding. Rashi, citing Bereshit Rabbah, takes it as a pledge that the food would not spoil and that the wicked would not harm Noah.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): a covenant was needed so that the food would not rot or spoil and that the wicked of the generation would not kill him. A reading of what the covenant covers; the English leaves the content open and records this.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'the men by themselves and the women by themselves'; from this they were forbidden marital relations in the ark. A homily on the order of the list.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: a sign that God had sworn to Noah that he and his sons would not die in the flood, though this was not stated before (compare Deuteronomy 1:22). וַהֲקִמֹתִי means 'I will fulfil my oath'. The view closest to his own is that this covenant alludes to the rainbow. בְּרִית is an agreement chosen by two parties, from בְּרוּ לָכֶם אִישׁ; others take it as a boundary cut.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: the plain sense is a covenant of survival: that Noah and his household and two of every kind would live and come out alive.
- Sforno: the covenant is made after the flood (אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל).
- Radak: the covenant that I make with you, that you and all who are with you will be saved from the waters, I will confirm for you.

Grammar:

- The verse begins with two phrases in a row, וּמִכׇּל־הָחַי מִכׇּל־בָּשָׂר: the general term, and its explanation.
- שְׁנַיִם מִכֹּל 'two from each' is the distributive: two of every kind.
- The verb תָּבִיא is a hifil imperfect: Noah must bring them in; the infinitive לְהַחֲיֹת gives the purpose.
- זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה יִהְיוּ: a plural verb for a pair; the subject is the 'two'.
- The telisha gedola on הָחַי and the gershayim on בָּשָׂר divide the opening phrase.

Note: The verb in יִהְיוּ is plural, agreeing with שְׁנַיִם. לְהַחֲיֹת אִתָּךְ: the object is implied: the animals are kept alive with Noah, and the English supplies 'them'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): 'even demons'. A homily on the scope of 'every living thing'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: from the smallest of them, not fewer than two, one male and one female. The English 'two of each'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: after saying 'two', the text explains that they are male and female. After the general 'of all the living, of all flesh', it lists the particular kinds: birds, cattle, and creeping things of the ground, the last covering the wild animals, small and great, born of male and female. Excluded are all creatures born without the mating of two, and so are the water creatures. The fish too is called 'flesh' (Numbers 11:21–22), so 'all flesh' alone could have included them.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: תָּבִיא is a command to Noah not to leave them but to bring them with him, to keep alive the seed of every kind. The English 'you shall bring'.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: it is a miracle that the ark held them; it was made large so that people would see it and repent.
- Radak on תָּבִיא: once they come of themselves in front of the ark, Noah brings them in; on לְהַחֲיֹת: Noah provides their food day by day.
- Onkelos: 'two of all you shall bring into the ark, to be kept alive with you; male and female they shall be'.

- שְׁנַיִם מִכֹּל יָבֹאוּ אֵלֶיךָ: the verb is now 'come' (qal) where verse 19 had 'bring' (hifil): they come to him.
- The infinitive לְהַחֲיוֹת is hifil: 'to keep alive'.
- The verse picks up the list that verse 19 summarised with the 'all flesh' phrase.

The English gives the plural 'their kind' for the first two phrases and 'its kind' for the third; the Hebrew has the singular suffix each time.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): those that clung to their own kinds and did not corrupt their way came of themselves; and whatever the ark took in he brought in. The English 'will come to you'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יָבֹאוּ אֵלֶיךָ means that they will come of themselves, and he will not have to search for them on the islands or hunt every kind of bird; he is to prepare food for all. The English 'will come to you'.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: the animals come of themselves two by two, but those taken for sacrifice (seven of each clean kind) Noah took himself.
- Radak: הַבְּהֵמָה includes the wild animals, since the two classes overlap.
- Onkelos: 'from the fowl according to its kind and from the cattle according to its kind and from all the creeping things of the earth according to its kind, two of each will come to you to be kept alive'.

- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: now take various foods for the various kinds; it adds detail, not a different reading.

Grammar:

- The wayyiqtol וַיַּעַשׂ narrates; the closing כֵּן עָשָׂה is a qatal that sums up.
- The etnaḥta on נֹחַ divides the report 'Noah did' from its measure, 'according to all that God commanded him'.
- The telisha gedola on כְּכֹל is a disjunctive accent of low rank. It is prepositive, written on the first letter of the word, and is written again on the stressed syllable.
- אֹתוֹ is the object marker with a 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'him'.
- Obedience is stated twice, in וַיַּעַשׂ נֹחַ and in כֵּן עָשָׂה, around the clause כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים.

Note: The English keeps the Hebrew order, with 'so he did' at the end. Ramban: the double statement, 'Noah did' and 'so he did', shows that he left out nothing of all he was commanded. Rashi takes the doing as the building of the ark; Ramban and Radak include the gathering of the food.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'this is the building of the ark': the making that Noah did is the construction of the ark.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: Noah both built the ark and gathered the food; the repetition 'so he did' shows he omitted nothing.
- Radak (records): Radak: he made the ark exactly as commanded, in length, width, height, nests, and the food he put in it.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'and Noah did according to all that the LORD commanded him; so he did'.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos has יְיָ ('the LORD') for אֱלֹהִים; this is Targum Onkelos's rendering, not a variant of the Hebrew.
