Grammar:

- אֹתְךָ is the object marker with a suffix, fronted before the verb; it stresses 'you, and no one else'.
- בֹּא־אַתָּה uses an independent pronoun after the imperative for emphasis.
- The etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה separates the command from its reason.
- צַדִּיק is the predicate of the object: 'I saw you (as) righteous'.

Note: Rashi stresses that the text says only 'righteous', not 'righteous and blameless' as in 6:9: a person is praised in part to his face, in full behind his back. Ramban and Sforno hold the emphatic 'you' implies that the household is saved for his sake only. The English keeps 'you' plain; the emphasis goes in the notes.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the verse does not say 'righteous and blameless'; one says part of a man's praise in his presence and all of it in his absence (Genesis Rabbah). The English says only 'righteous'.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: Noah is told to enter with his whole household, and the text shows that they are saved in his merit alone, since it does not say 'I have seen you all righteous'.
- Radak (records): Radak: it is fitting that you and all your household escape the flood so that the world is settled again.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'enter, you and all the people of your house, into the ark, for I have seen you righteous (zakkai) before me in this generation'.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: 'you, not your house' (the household is saved only because of him).

#### Genesis 7:2

> מִכֹּ֣ל ׀ הַבְּהֵמָ֣ה הַטְּהוֹרָ֗ה תִּֽקַּח־לְךָ֛ שִׁבְעָ֥ה שִׁבְעָ֖ה אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשְׁתּ֑וֹ וּמִן־הַבְּהֵמָ֡ה אֲ֠שֶׁ֠ר לֹ֣א טְהֹרָ֥ה הִ֛וא שְׁנַ֖יִם אִ֥ישׁ וְאִשְׁתּֽוֹ׃

Grammar:

- תִּקַּח is an imperfect used as a command; the accent on לְךָ is tevir.
- שִׁבְעָה שִׁבְעָה is distributive repetition. It can mean seven individuals of each kind or seven pairs; the text itself says 'a male and his mate' after it.
- אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ are the words for a human husband and wife, here applied to animals (Radak: a figurative use).
- לֹא טְהֹרָה הִוא ('that is not clean') stands for 'unclean'. Radak: Scripture often puts a quality in the negative, as in כִּי לֹא טָהוֹר הוּא (1 Sam 20:26), and the sense is the same; the rabbis learned from this verse that one should not utter an unseemly word.

Note: The English leaves the ambiguity in 'seven each' (seven individuals or seven pairs). Radak reads seven pairs; Rashi says only that the extras are for a sacrifice at exit. 'Clean' is not defined in the text; Rashi reads it as 'destined to be clean for Israel', Sforno as 'fit for sacrifice', and Radak that God told Noah the signs of cleanness or that he recognized them by their coming in sevens.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'the clean' means those destined to be clean for Israel, and from this we learn that Noah studied Torah; the English takes it as simply 'clean'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the seven each are so that he can offer a sacrifice from them on leaving the ark; it explains 'seven' and does not change the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: he says now that Noah should bring seven pairs of each clean animal and one pair (or two) of the unclean; he asks how Noah knew which was clean and gives two answers.
- Radak (records): Radak: אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ means male and female, said figuratively; when the pairs are alike the text says 'a woman to her sister', and when they differ as male and female it says 'man and his wife'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the text says 'not clean' rather than 'unclean' as it often does, and the rabbis learned from it that one should not speak a foul word.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'seven seven, male and female' and 'two, male and female' for the unclean.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: at that time all clean animals were fit for sacrifice, as the rabbis said, and in their food-nature unlike 'you shall be defiled by them'.

- הַיְקוּם is rare: here, 7:23 and Deut 11:6. Ibn Ezra says it occurs only in this section; he and Radak take it as a general word for every living being.
- The verse uses אֲדָמָה (ground), not אֶרֶץ, for what is wiped out.

Note: The BDB entry gives `substance, existence` for הַיְקוּם; the English 'living thing' follows Ibn Ezra, 'a general term for every living being on the earth' and Radak ('all that is on the face of the ground among living beings'). Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: these seven days are the mourning for Methuselah the righteous; God spared his honor and delayed the punishment; count his years and you find they end in the six hundredth year of Noah (Sanhedrin 108). The English gives only 'seven more days'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: what is 'still'? Another period after, added to the 120 years.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: forty days matches the forming of the embryo, since they corrupted themselves; a homily that does not bear on the translation.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: on the seventh day He will bring rain, and it will last to the end of forty days; this was on the tenth of the second month. His closing words, that 'the middle returns to the front, and it is a secret', are an astronomical remark that does not bear on the words. He reads 'in seven more days' as the English does.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַיְקוּם is found only in this section; its root is among verbs whose first letter is not complete (like כרוב), or among hollow verbs, and it is a general term for every living thing on the ground.
- Radak (records): Radak: Noah is to enter the ark seven days before the flood to prepare places and food; the rabbis say the seven days are for Methuselah's mourning.
- Radak (follows): Radak: הַיְקוּם is general for everything alive on the ground; the root is קום with a letter yod added, as in רִיבָה.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'every living thing' means what is on dry land and on the ground, not fish or what is in the ark.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'for after a time of seven more days I am bringing rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every standing thing that I made from upon the face of the earth'.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders הַיְקוּם by its cognate יְקוּמָא and אֲדָמָה by אַרְעָא, his usual equivalent; neither is a variant of the Hebrew.

Grammar:

- The date is a series of ב phrases: year, month, day of the month, with the time clause leading to the main verbs נִבְקְעוּ and נִפְתָּחוּ.
- Both verbs are Niphal qatal, plural, passive: 'were split', 'were opened'.
- מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם רַבָּה: the springs of the great deep; תְּהוֹם is also found with the feminine adjective here, and Ibn Ezra notes it is both masculine and feminine.
- The symmetry of the verse sets the springs of the earth below against the windows of the sky above.

Note: 'The great deep' keeps תְּהוֹם רַבָּה; Rashi's note sees measure for measure in רַבָּה. Of the two second-month readings in Rashi, the English says only 'second month'; the commentators' disagreement over which month that is does not affect the English words.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: R. Eliezer says the second month is Marheshvan; R. Joshua says it is Iyyar. The English says only 'the second month'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: נבקעו means that they were split open to let out their waters.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: measure for measure, they sinned with 'great' (רבה) wickedness of man and were punished by a 'great' deep. The English keeps 'great'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מַעְיְנֹת here is in the construct state (סמוך), bound to תהום; in 'when there were no springs' (באין מעינות, Prov 8:24) the same word stands alone (מוכרת). A point of form: 'springs of the great deep'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: תהום is both masculine and feminine, as in 'the deep raised it up' (תהום רוממתהו, Ezek 31:4). The text does not mention rivers, since they come from the springs. When the springs split the waters rose; the windows of the storehouses in heaven opened and the waters came down, and the earth was thrown into confusion, with no telling day from night, as 'day and night shall not cease' (8:22) shows. When the rain stopped Noah knew that forty days and forty nights had passed, because God revealed it to him.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: ארבות is as in 'behold, the LORD makes windows' (2 Kings 7:2); 'storehouse' and 'window' are said in human terms. Some take the aleph as a root letter, like כבודות; others as added, like the aleph of אגורת (1 Sam 2:36), from a doubled root. On the seventeenth, when the flood began, Noah and his household entered the ark and brought in the animals and birds; צפור is a general term for whatever has a wing, and the wonder is that all came of themselves, two by two.

Apparatus:

- Rashi's R. Eliezer and R. Joshua differ over the month; Radak reports the same dispute.

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'on that very day' teaches that Noah's generation threatened to break the ark and kill him if they saw him enter; God brought him in before all eyes. A homiletic point on the idiom.

Grammar:

- וְהַבָּאִים is a participle with the article, 'the ones coming', the subject of בָּאוּ.
- The sentence has a long subject separated from its verb by 'male and female from all flesh'.
- כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים recalls the command of 6:19-20 and 7:2-3.
- בַּעֲדוֹ: בְּעַד means 'about, behind'; Rashi reads it as כְּנֶגֶד, 'facing, against': the LORD shut the ark about him, against the water. This is the only place in the unit where the name יְהוָה appears.

Note: Rashi gives two readings of בעדו: the homiletic one (bears and lions ringed the ark) and the plain sense (he shut it against the water). The English follows the plain sense. The name is God (אֱלֹהִים) in the command and the LORD in the shutting.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: by the midrash, He protected him so that people would not break the ark, ringing it with bears and lions that killed them; the plain sense is that He shut [the ark] כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, 'facing him', against the water. Every בְּעַד in Scripture means כְּנֶגֶד, as in 'pray בְּעַד your servants' (1 Sam 12:19), 'facing your servants'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַבָּאִים means those who entered the ark.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'shut behind him' here is praise: the LORD shielded him so that not even a place in the ark opened, since otherwise all would have died at once; elsewhere סגר can be negative (Job 12:14, 3:23).
- Radak (follows): Radak: He shielded him so that not even one hole opened in the ark in the force of the rains.

- The wayyiqtols וַיִּרְבּוּ וַיִּשְׂאוּ וַתָּרׇם follow one another as a chain of consequences.
- וַתָּרׇם is a short form of the Qal of רום with feminine subject (the ark).

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the ark sank eleven cubits in the water, like a loaded ship that is partly submerged; the verses that follow (15 cubits) prove it. The English 'rose above the earth' is compatible with this.
- Radak (records): Radak: the forty days are days and nights; the night is included in the day, as in 'there was evening and there was morning'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: when the waters of the forty days and the springs had increased, they had the power to lift the ark.

- גבר and רבה are close in sense: 'be strong' and 'be many'. 7:17 used רבה; this verse has both; 7:19-20 use גבר alone.

- Radak (follows): Radak: this verse adds to the increase of the waters; they became stronger than before.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: the ark moved by the force of the surge that came from below.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מאד מאד, said twice, is a degree beyond which there is none. Since 'all the high mountains were covered' has been said, why repeat 'and the mountains were covered' (7:20)? It means that every high mountain was covered by the water, and the fifteen cubits covered those same mountains. We believe the words of our God and leave aside the vain talk of men about a high mountain in the kingdom of Greece.
- Radak (follows): Radak: there are two increases here: the first 'increased very' and now 'prevailed very, very', so that all the high mountains were covered.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיִּגְוַע means 'it had already died'; the form is common in the Torah (compare Deut 3:23 and Ps 78:24).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיִּגְוַע means death; the word רֶמֶשׂ includes bird, beast, wild animal, swarming thing and human. He also suggests that 'all in whose nostrils was the breath of life' refers back to humans, since נְשָׁמָה is found only of humans.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: 'and all humankind' comes last to say that even a man who might find a place of refuge died.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: even the Nephilim, who climbed the high mountains, were covered and drowned.

- Radak (follows): Radak: but the fish of the sea did not die, since their rearing is in the water and they are not with man.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: אַךְ נֹחַ means 'Noah alone', and that is the plain sense; he adds the homily that Noah groaned and spat blood from the work of tending the animals, or that a lion bit him.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיִּמָּחוּ מִן הָאָרֶץ means that their names were wiped out from the earth, since they left no offspring; וַיִּשָּׁאֶר means only Noah and those with him remained, a full answer to those who say the flood was not over all the earth.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the doubling may be for the birds and some creeping things, to say that no eggs of theirs were left in any tree or under the ground; or the verse may be read 'all, from human to bird, were wiped out from the earth; only Noah was left'. The rabbis read 'he wiped out' of this world and 'they were wiped out from the earth' of the world to come.

Apparatus:

- 7:23.20 vowels: WLC reads וַיִשָּׁאֶר without the dagesh in yod; the base text וַיִּשָּׁאֶר is followed.
- וַיִּשָּׁ֧אֶר: WLC reads וַיִשָּׁ֧אֶר (vowels)

- Pashta is written on the last letter of its word. On רוּחַ it is written a second time, on רוּ, because the stress falls on the first syllable: the pataḥ under ח is a furtive pataḥ.
- וַיָּשֹׁכּוּ is the Qal wayyiqtol of the doubled root שׁכך, the verb of Esther 7:10 (וַחֲמַת הַמֶּלֶךְ שָׁכָכָה); the dagesh in the כ makes up for the root's missing second letter (Ibn Ezra). The sense is 'settle, abate'.

Note: The English keeps 'God' for אֱלֹהִים by decision, even though Rashi reads it as the attribute of justice turned to mercy. 'Noah' stands for Noah with his sons and wives, as Ibn Ezra says. 'Wind' (not 'spirit') because the verb is Hiphil of 'pass over' and the object is something that blows over the earth, as Ibn Ezra ('he made it pass continually') and Radak take it; Rashi's reading, a spirit of comfort passing before God concerning the affairs of the earth, is recorded.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: this name, אֱלֹהִים, is the attribute of justice, turned to mercy by the prayer of the righteous; the wickedness of the wicked turns mercy to justice. A homily on the divine name.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: what did God remember for the animals? Their merit: they had not corrupted their ways before the flood, and they had not mated in the ark (שֶׁלֹּא שִׁמְּשׁוּ בַּתֵּבָה). A homily.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: a spirit of comfort and calm (רוּחַ תַּנְחוּמִין וַהֲנָחָה) passed before God: he reads רוּחַ as God's disposition, not a wind. The English follows the plain wind over the earth (Ibn Ezra, Radak) and records Rashi.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: עַל הָאָרֶץ means concerning the affairs of the earth. The English reads the plain 'over the earth'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיָּשֹׁכּוּ is like כְּשֹׁךְ חֲמַת הַמֶּלֶךְ, a word for the settling of anger. The English: subsided.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: his sons and the women are included in Noah, who is the main one. The English names Noah.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it includes beasts of the field, birds, and every creeping thing; the sense of 'remembered' is the oath God swore to Noah. The English has 'every living creature'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: he made it pass continually. The English has the causative verb without an end point.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: they rested and no longer prevailed; so too the king's anger subsided (Esther 7:10). The dagesh in the כ makes up for the missing second letter of the root (the ע of the pattern פעל), and both verbs are Qal. The English: the waters subsided.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the mention of Noah is for his merit; the mention of the animals is not for merit but because God remembered his word at the creation and wished the species to continue.
- Radak (records): Radak: the wind stood against the water so that it could no longer rise, and the water settled and went down by its nature.

#### Genesis 8:2

**The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the sky were shut, and the rain from the sky was held back.**

- Two Niphal wayyiqtols (וַיִּסָּכְרוּ, וַיִּכָּלֵא) describe the end of the flood as passives: no agent is named.
- The Hebrew has no 'all' here, unlike 7:11 (כָּל מַעְיְנֹת): Rashi draws the lesson from this.
- סכר and סגר are two forms of one meaning (Ibn Ezra, Radak).

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: when they opened, the text has כָּל מַעְיְנֹת; here it has no כָּל, for those useful to the world were left, such as the hot springs of Tiberias. The English likewise has no 'all'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיִּכָּלֵא means was held back, as in לֹא תִכְלָא רַחֲמֶיךָ (Psalm 40) and לֹא יִכְלֶה מִמְּךָ (Genesis 23).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיִּסָּכְרוּ is like וַיִּסָּגְרוּ; kaf does not interchange with gimel, rather these are two roots with one meaning.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it was shut up inside the storehouse. The English: held back.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: no more rain fell until they left the ark; the heavens were like iron.

- הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב: two infinitive absolutes after a finite verb express continuing action (compare 8:5, הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר).
- The tevir on הַמַּיִם and the etnaḥta on וָשׁוֹב divide the verse after the first clause; the zaqef gadol on מִקְצֵה sets the number apart.
- וַיַּחְסְרוּ is a stative Qal wayyiqtol of a verb with a stative vowel (חָסֵר).
- The word order of the second clause puts the verb before its subject: וַיַּחְסְרוּ הַמַּיִם.

Note: 'Steadily' translates the idiom; the words 'going and returning' are in the literal line. The English follows the timing of Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak: the waters began to decrease at the end of the hundred and fifty days. Ramban joins מִקְצֵה with the following 'the ark came to rest'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they began to decrease on the first of Sivan. How? The rains stopped on 27 Kislev; there are three more of Kislev, twenty-nine of Tevet, and so on to one hundred and fifty.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיָּשֻׁבוּ means below the earth as usual, at the end of the hundred and fifty days; he rejects the attempts to compute the months by the sun or by intercalation. The English: steadily, at the end of the days.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the waters were decreasing little by little until the ground was dry; the words מִקְצֵה חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם join to וַתָּנַח הַתֵּבָה: on that day the decrease was great.
- Radak (follows): Radak: little by little, until they decreased at the end of a hundred and fifty days; they began to decrease on 1 Sivan, when the rising stopped.

- וַתָּנַח: the verb is feminine, as תֵּבָה is feminine; a play on נֹחַ, whose name comes from נוח.

- The zaqef qaton on הַשְּׁבִיעִי and the etnaḥta on לַחֹדֶשׁ separate the date from the place.

Note: The English does not say which reckoning gives 'the seventh month'. Rashi and Radak count from the stopping of the rain (Sivan); Ramban attributes another reckoning to Ibn Ezra and others. Rashi's inference that the ark sank eleven cubits is a calculation from the days and cubits.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: the seventh month is Sivan, the seventh from the stopping of the rains in Kislev. The English leaves the starting point of the count open.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: from here you learn that the ark was sunk eleven cubits in the water, by a calculation from the exposure of the mountain tops at a rate of one cubit in four days. A computation that does not bear on the words.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: rejects Rashi's counts as not suiting the wording and says the sinking is not proved.
- Radak (records): Radak: the seventh month is Sivan, the seventh from the rain's stopping; the ark rested on the seventeenth of it.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the mountains of Ararat may be the high ones, or the ark was in that region; some are lower, since not all were seen until the tenth month.

- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: Noah fixed the first of the month without seeing the moon, since the window was not yet open; the tenth month is counted from the day of the flood, and he sent the raven on the tenth of Shevat. The English leaves the reckoning open.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the order is inverted: the waters kept diminishing until the mountain tops were seen in the tenth month, which is Tammuz.
- Radak (follows): Radak: they kept diminishing, as in 'the creatures ran and returned' (Ezekiel 1:14).
- Radak (follows): Radak: it does not say all the water was gone in the tenth month; only the tops of the mountains were seen then, and the decrease went on after.

- וַיֵּצֵא יָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב: a finite verb followed by two infinitive absolutes; the pair gives continued, repeated motion.
- The etnaḥta on הָעֹרֵב ends the first clause; the zaqef qaton on וָשׁוֹב sets off 'went out and back' from the time clause.
- עַד יְבֹשֶׁת הַמַּיִם: עַד with an infinitive construct (feminine form of יבשׁ) forms a time clause.
- מֵעַל is a compound preposition, 'from upon', so 'from off'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi reads יָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב as the raven going and circling round the ark and not going on its errand, because it suspected Noah about its mate (Sanhedrin 108b). The English 'back and forth' fits this but does not say it.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'its plain sense is as it sounds' (the raven went and came until the waters dried); the Aggadic reading that the raven was kept for a later errand in Elijah's drought (1 Kings 17) is homily and does not bear on the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: the raven would eat carrion and bring back flesh if the waters were low; Noah saw it go in and out of its nest until the waters dried.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos has the raven 'going out and returning' until the waters dried from the earth.

Apparatus:

- Rashi and Radak differ on where the raven went; the Hebrew gives no destination.

- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'and he sent the dove from with him to see whether the waters had lightened (הֲקַלִּיאוּ)'.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: if the waters had lightened, the dove would nest in the mountains and towers as is her custom.

Commentary:

- Ramban (follows): Ramban: birds do not usually rest on the peaks of high mountains, where there are no trees, all the more so while water covered the face of all the earth; so the dove found no resting place that suited her. When the trees appeared she went off on her own, for doves nest in their branches.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: even the visible mountaintops were still very damp, so that even there she could not rest.

Grammar:

- וַיֹּסֶף שַׁלַּח: a verb of adding with an infinitive means doing something again; 'he added to send' is 'he sent again'.
- וַיָּחֶל is a hard form. Rashi: a term of waiting (לְשׁוֹן הַמְתָּנָה), as וְיִחֵלּוּ in Job 29:21. Radak: Hiphil of חול, 'wait', as וַיָּחִילוּ in Judg 3:25. Ibn Ezra prefers 'he began' (from תְּחִלָּה; compare וַיָּחֶל נֹחַ, 'Noah began', 9:20), since from תּוֹחֶלֶת he would expect וייחל or ייחל, but he allows an irregular form.
- שִׁבְעַת יָמִים אֲחֵרִים: the number is in construct before the plural noun; אֲחֵרִים 'other' means a second week.

Note: The English 'waited' follows Rashi and the context. The lexicon sense is the nearest the entry offers and may belong rather to יָחַל; that is a limit of the data.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיָּחֶל is a term of waiting, like 'to me they listened and waited (וְיִחֵלּוּ)' (Job 29:21); there are many such in Scripture.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: in his view וַיָּחֶל comes from תְּחִלָּה, 'beginning' (he began another seven days); had it come from תּוֹחֶלֶת, 'waiting', it would be וייחל like וייקץ, or ייחל like וישב (37:1). He allows that it may be a word irregular in grammar. The English follows Rashi's 'waited' and records Ibn Ezra's 'began'.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra dates the sending to the twenty-fourth of Shevat; a calendar remark that does not bear on the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: the root is חו״ל in the Hiphil, like 'they waited until they were ashamed' (Judges 3:25).
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'he waited (וְאוֹרִיךְ) another seven days and again sent the dove from the ark'.

Apparatus:

- וַיָּחֶל: Rashi and Radak 'he waited'; Ibn Ezra prefers 'he began (another seven days)', from תְּחִלָּה, and allows 'waited' only as an irregular form. The pack parses the form as Piel of חוּל; Radak calls it Hiphil.

Others cited by Ibn Ezra take it as a noun, 'leaf'.
- The dove is feminine (בְּפִיהָ); Rashi, who reads the masculine form טָרָף, holds that the bird was male.
- וַיֵּדַע נֹחַ כִּי־קַלּוּ: the verb of knowing takes a כִּי clause; קַלּוּ echoes הֲקַלּוּ of 8:8.

Note: 'freshly plucked' follows Radak and the BDB gloss; Rashi's 'snatched' (חָטַף) is close in sense. Beak is the bird's mouth. The feminine pronoun is kept.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'I say it was male', and that is why the text speaks of it sometimes in the masculine (טָרָף) and sometimes in the feminine (בְּפִיהָ): the feminine because every dove in Scripture is spoken of in the feminine (Song 5:12; Ezek 7:16; Hos 7:11). The English keeps the Hebrew's feminine 'her'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: טָרָף means 'snatched' (חָטַף); the Aggadah takes it as 'food' and בְּפִיהָ as 'speech', the dove saying that she would rather have bitter food from God than sweet from flesh and blood. The homily is not adopted.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: some say טָרָף is a noun doubling עֲלֵה in sense, 'leaf' (cf. טַרְפֵּי צִמְחָהּ, Ezek 17:9), citing the qamets under the resh as in זָהָב. He holds rather that the ב of בְּפִיהָ is superfluous and טָרָף is a verb with qamets, as כִּי הוּא טָרָף (Hos 6:1), 'her mouth had plucked (it)'; or else that טָרָף is an adjective like חָכָם with a passive sense, like טָרוּף. Either way the dove tore the leaf off, which 'plucked' carries.
- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban infers from the plain text that the trees were not uprooted or destroyed in the Flood; the Midrash holds that the leaf came from elsewhere. This bears on the setting, not on the words.
- Radak (follows): Radak: טָרָף is an adjective in place of a passive, like טָרוּף: the dove tore it from the olive tree; Noah saw that it was torn, not found floating.
- Radak (follows): Radak: קַלּוּ means 'diminished', for a small thing is light and a large one heavy.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'a plucked (תְּבִיר) olive leaf in her mouth'.

Apparatus:

- טָרָף: adjective 'plucked' (BDB, Radak, Onkelos תְּבִיר, and Ibn Ezra's second view); verb 'snatched, plucked' (Rashi חָטַף; Ibn Ezra's preferred view, with the ב of בְּפִיהָ superfluous); noun 'leaf' (others cited by Ibn Ezra). The Midrash cited by Rashi takes it as 'food'.

- וַיִּיָּחֶל is Niphal (not Hithpael, which would have a patah under the yod); the root is יחל, 'wait'.
- לֹא־יָסְפָה שׁוּב: 'she did not add to return', the same idiom of repetition as in 8:10, now negative.
- The disjunctive accents divide the verse into three: the waiting, the sending, the result.
- The two forms וַיָּחֶל (8:10) and וַיִּיָּחֶל (8:12) differ in stem but say the same.

Note: The dove's failure to return is not explained in the text; Radak reads it as the dove finding rest.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: this is the same as וַיָּחֶל but in a reflexive stem: the first is 'he waited', the second 'he was patient'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: a Niphal form, as in וַיִּלָּחֶם and וַיִּצָּמֶד; the root is complete with the yod.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: עוֹד means 'forever', as in 'his uncleanness is still on him' and 'all the days of the earth'. The English 'any more' is close to this.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the form is Niphal from יח״ל; had it been Hithpael, the yod would be open (pataḥ), and it is qamets.
- Radak (records): Radak: Noah knew then that the ground was dry and the dove had found rest on the earth and in many trees, so she did not come back.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'and she did not again return to him any more'.

> וַ֠יְהִ֠י בְּאַחַ֨ת וְשֵׁשׁ־מֵא֜וֹת שָׁנָ֗ה בָּֽרִאשׁוֹן֙ בְּאֶחָ֣ד לַחֹ֔דֶשׁ חָֽרְב֥וּ הַמַּ֖יִם מֵעַ֣ל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיָּ֤סַר נֹ֙חַ֙ אֶת־מִכְסֵ֣ה הַתֵּבָ֔ה וַיַּ֕רְא וְהִנֵּ֥ה חָֽרְב֖וּ פְּנֵ֥י הָֽאֲדָמָֽה׃

- The date is given in Hebrew order: year, month, day. 'the first' (הָרִאשׁוֹן) is the first month; the day is 'one' (אֶחָד), used for 'the first'.
- חָרְבוּ הַמַּיִם and חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה: the verb חרב (dry up) is used of the waters and then of the surface of the ground; in 8:14 the verb is the stronger יבשׁ.
- וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה: 'he saw, and behold': a narrative view of what Noah saw when the cover was open.
- The telisha gedola on וַיְהִי is a prepositive disjunctive accent, printed at the start of the word and again on the stressed syllable; it sets וַיְהִי apart from the date that follows.

Note: The first month is Tishrei or Nisan (Rashi: R. Eliezer or R. Joshua). The text says only 'first'. The English keeps חרב as 'dried up' and יבשׁ in 8:14 as 'dry', following Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the difference.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'the first month' is Tishrei according to R. Eliezer and Nisan according to R. Joshua (Rosh Hashanah 11b). The English says only 'the first month'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: חָרְבוּ means it became like mud, for a crust formed on the upper surface. This is why 'dried up' here is not yet fully dry.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra dates the dove's last sending to the first of Adar; the comment is about chronology and does not bear on the English.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the ground was still soft, so a foot could not tread on it; only its surface had dried. Full dryness comes in verse 14.
- Radak (follows): Radak: with Tishrei, the first month, Noah entered his six hundred and first year, and on the seventeenth of the second month his year in the ark was complete. Though the face of the ground had dried, there was still mud beneath and it was not fit to walk on; so Noah did not go out, but waited for God to command him, as He had commanded him to go in.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'in the six hundred and first year, in the first, on the first of the month the waters dried (נְגוּבוּ) from the earth'.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: Noah thought the surplus moisture in the air had dried; a remark on his reasoning.

A point of chronology that does not bear on the English.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: יָבְשָׁה means it became fully dry as it should be (גָּרִיד כְּהִלְכָתָהּ).
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the second month is Marheshvan; the rabbis say the days are the ten extra of the solar year. A calendar note.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry (יַבִּישַׁת)'.

- וַיְדַבֵּר is a Piel wayyiqtol; the merkha is on the verb, the tipḥa on אֱלֹהִים.

- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos renders closely: 'And the LORD spoke with Noah, saying.' It does not bear on the English.

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| מִן | from | מִן־ |  | preposition |  |
| הַתֵּבָ֑ה | the ark | ה: the + תֵּבָה |  | particle (definite article) + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |
| אַתָּ֕ה | you | אַתָּ֫ה | אנת | pronoun (personal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) |  |

| וּנְשֵֽׁי | and wives of — construct plural נְשֵׁי, the irregular plural of אִשָּׁה; joined by maqqef to the next word | ו: and + אִשָּׁה | אנשׁ | conjunction + noun (common, feminine, plural, construct) | 2 |

- צֵא is the imperative of יצא with the first radical dropped; the tipḥa on it and the etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה divide the command from the list of those who go.
- The list pairs each man with his wife: 'you and your wife', then 'your sons and your sons' wives'. In 6:18 and 7:7 the men and the women are listed in separate groups on entering; here the couples are paired, the point Rashi and Radak draw from the verse. The accents divide the list step by step: the zaqef gadol on אַתָּה sets 'you' apart, the tipḥa on בָנֶיךָ sets off אִתָּךְ, and the tevir on וְאִשְׁתְּךָ divides 'and your wife' from the sons and their wives.
- The construct plural נְשֵׁי־בָנֶיךָ is 'wives of your sons'.

Note: The wording is plain. The couples are named together here, unlike the entry (6:18, 7:7), which Rashi and Radak take as the point of the verse.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'A man and his wife: here He permitted them marital relations.' This is an inference from the pairing of husband and wife and does not change the English wording.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak joins the women to the men to show that relations were now permitted, as the rabbis said. Not a matter of translation.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos translates word for word.

Grammar:

- The object (כָּל־הַחַיָּה ...) comes before the verb הַיְצֵא; the zaqef and revia divide the long object from its specification, and the etnaḥta closes the command.
- הַיְצֵא is read (qere) as a Hiphil imperative; the ketiv הוצא is the same form spelled with a vav in place of the yod.
- The three weqatal verbs וְשָׁרְצוּ וּפָרוּ וְרָבוּ follow the imperative and give the purpose of the going out; the echo of 1:22 and 9:1 is clear.
- רֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ is a figura etymologica, 'creeping thing that creeps'.

Note: The ketiv/qere is kept in the token note. Following Ibn Ezra's grammar (הַיְצֵא like הַשְׁלֵם, a Hiphil), the English uses 'Bring out'. For וְשָׁרְצוּ the English follows Ibn Ezra's gloss יולידו 'let them bear young', which Radak (רבוי התולדה) and Onkelos (ויתילדון) share, and on which Rashi's deduction about the ark rests: 'breed abundantly' keeps both the teeming of שׁרץ and the bearing of young. The literal line keeps 'swarm'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: the ketiv is הוֹצֵא, the qere הַיְצֵא. The qere means 'tell them to go out'; the ketiv means 'if they do not want to go out, bring them out yourself'. The English keeps the causative 'bring out' and records both.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: וְשָׁרְצוּ בָאָרֶץ means 'on the earth, and not in the ark', which shows that the animals and birds were forbidden to breed in the ark. This is a deduction and the English does not state it.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַיְצֵא is like הַשְׁלֵם, and so 'הַיְשַׁר לפני דרכך' (Ps 5:9): a Hiphil imperative, which the English follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra glosses ושרצו by a single word, יולידו, 'they shall bear young'. The English 'breed abundantly' follows him.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the ketiv has a vav in place of the yod; the first radical vav is silent as is usual, while the qere shows the yod as is normal. He glosses 'bring them out with you as you brought them in with you'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: as at the first creation; the verb שרץ speaks of multiplying offspring and is used there only of fish.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos renders ושרצו by יתילדון, 'let them breed', with אפיק for the imperative.

Apparatus:

- 8:17.14 ketiv-qere: ketiv הוצא (Hiphil imperative with vav), qere הַיְצֵא (with yod).
- הַיְצֵ֣א: ketiv reads הוצא (ketiv-qere)

- אִתּוֹ 'with him' (silluq) closes the verse.

- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: כל רומש על הארץ includes cattle and wild beasts.
- Radak (follows): Radak glosses 'by their kinds', each kind by itself.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos renders לזרעיתהון 'by their families', word for word.

- מִכֹּל is partitive: he took only some of each clean kind, not all of them.
- The adjectives הַטְּהֹרָה and הַטָּהוֹר agree in gender with בְּהֵמָה (feminine) and עוֹף (masculine).
- The pashta after מִכֹּל and the zaqef qaton after הַטָּהוֹר set the two lists apart.

Note: The English 'offered burnt offerings' keeps the Hebrew's plural עֹלֹת. The orthography הַטְּהֹרָה and הַטָּהוֹר (WLC reads הַטְּהוֹרָה and הַטָּהֹר) is only spelling.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Noah said that the Holy One had not commanded him to bring in seven of each clean kind except in order to offer a sacrifice from them. The English 'some of every' reflects this taking of a portion for sacrifice.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the clean beasts are ten (kinds); we do not know the number of the clean birds, since there are more of them than of the unclean; and he built the altar on one of the mountains of Ararat (בְּאַחַד הָרֵי אֲרָרָט). It does not bear on the English.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak discusses where Noah built the altar: where he left the ark, or elsewhere after the ark moved, or on the site of the later altar in Jerusalem (Bereshit Rabbah 34).
- Radak (records): Radak: the clean wild animal is included in בהמה; he offered from all clean kinds, as thanks to God that they were saved from the flood.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the sages disagree whether he offered only whole burnt offerings or also peace offerings with them (Zevaḥim 116).
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos translates word for word, with 'offered up' for the Hiphil.

- 8:20.8 spelling: WLC reads הַטְּהוֹרָ֗ה; base הַטְּהֹרָ֗ה.

Grammar:

- The verse has two clauses of narration (וַיָּרַח, וַיֹּאמֶר) and then God's speech: two parallel vows, each opening לֹא־אֹסִף ... עוֹד, with a reason (כִּי ...) set between them.
- אֹסִף is a Hiphil imperfect of יסף; with an infinitive it means 'I will do again', so לֹא אֹסִף לְקַלֵּל is 'I will not again curse'.
- The segolta on הַנִּיחֹחַ (printed twice in this edition) closes the first clause, with the zarqa (zinor) on יְהֹוָה as a lesser divider within it. The etnaḥta on מִנְּעֻרָיו divides the verse: the first vow and its reason stand before it, and the second vow after it. The telisha gedola on אֹסִף and on כִּי is a minor disjunctive.
- יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם is a construct chain: 'the formation of the human heart'; the adjective רַע is the predicate, and מִנְּעֻרָיו 'from his youth' modifies it.
- The repeated אֹסִף עוֹד in two clauses is what Rashi takes as an oath.

Note: The notes follow Ibn Ezra on the grammar: וַיָּרַח is a figure of speech (the offering was accepted, as one smells a pleasing scent); אֶל־לִבּוֹ means 'with/to his heart', that is 'to himself'; לְקַלֵּל is a curse on the ground that came through man (cf. 3:17); יֵצֶר is what was formed in the human. For מִנְּעֻרָיו Rashi reads the defective spelling (מנעריו כְּתִיב) as from נִנְעַר 'shaken out' (from birth) and Ramban records both 'from the beginning of youth' and 'because of youth'; the English keeps the plain 'from his youth'. The quoted speech is set in double quotation marks in the English only.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: it is written מנעריו, without the vav, which he reads as from נִנְעַר: from the time he is shaken out (נִנְעַר) to leave his mother's womb, the evil inclination is placed in him. The English keeps the plain sense 'from his youth' and records his reading.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the doubling of 'I will not add' is for an oath; Isaiah 54:9 says 'as I swore ... the waters of Noah', and the only oath the Torah records is this doubling. The English repeats 'never again' in both vows, and the oath is noted here.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיָּרַח is on the pattern of 'וינח בכל גבול מצרים' (Ex 10:14), with a patah under the resh because of the guttural ח. God does not smell: the meaning is that He accepted the burnt offering and it pleased Him, as a person smells a sweet scent and it is pleasant. The English 'smelled' keeps the verb of the text.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַנִּיחֹחַ is from מְנוּחָה 'rest', and the ח is doubled like the pe of ונאפופיה; the sense is that it set down (הניח) His anger, or that it placed a higher strength at rest. The English 'soothing' follows this.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אֶל לִבּוֹ is like עִם לִבּוֹ, 'with his heart'; afterwards He revealed the secret to Noah, who was a prophet. The English 'to himself' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'I will not again curse' means as the curse came through man, since it is written 'cursed is the ground' (3:17). The English follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יֵצֶר is the nature that was formed in him. The English 'inclination' renders the sense of formation.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'I will not again' refers to the flood. The English follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the word עוֹד means 'for ever' or 'a second time', as in 'and he wept on his neck still' (Gen 46:29). The English 'never again' takes the second sense.
- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban: God did not reveal this to a prophet at that time, but later when He commanded Moses to write the Torah; 'because of the human' means the animals were punished on account of man.
- Ramban (records): Ramban gives two readings of the מ in מנעריו: 'from the beginning of youth', as the sages say, or 'because of' youth, which makes the evil of the heart come from youth. He also records 'like בנעריו'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the Torah speaks as men speak, as a figure; the offering was accepted with favour.
- Radak (follows): Radak: נִיחֹחַ is on the pattern of ניצוץ; the sense is that He set down (הניח) His anger in the world.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: God saw by His reason that the evil would not be many again, and that the whole would not be destroyed for the part.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: because of the human means that the wicked would end and the ground remain for the good.
- Radak (follows): Radak: it is called יֵצֶר because it is formed with the human; the evil inclination exists in a person before the good.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos renders: 'the LORD accepted his offering with favour, and said by His word, I will not again curse the earth on account of the sins of man, for the inclination of the heart of man is evil from his youth.'
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: the offering was then fit to be offered.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: after the flood the temperaments are weaker, so the power of reason does not shine in them from their youth as it did before.

Apparatus:

- 8:21 Ramban and Rashi read מנעריו differently: Rashi as 'from the shaking out of the womb', Ramban as 'from the beginning of youth' or 'because of youth'.

**For as long as the earth lasts, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never cease.**

Grammar:

- עֹד כָּל־יְמֵי הָאָרֶץ is a time clause, 'all the days of the earth still', with the etnaḥta marking its end; the plural verb יִשְׁבֹּתוּ at the end governs all the pairs.
- The eight nouns stand in four pairs of opposites: sowing and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, then day and night. Every noun after the first takes vav; in the second member of three pairs it is pointed וָ (וָחֹם, וָחֹרֶף, וָלַיְלָה), which binds the pair closely.
- יִשְׁבֹּתוּ is the Qal of שׁבת 'to cease'; the same root gives the Sabbath, 'the ceasing'.
- The unusual accents (pazer, telisha gedola, qadma) give the list a slow, rhythmical delivery.

Note: Rashi divides the year into six seasons of two months each (half Tishri to half Kislev for sowing, and so on); Ibn Ezra divides the year first in two (sowing and harvest) and then in four (cold and heat, summer and winter), which also fits the Hebrew pairs. The English keeps the six nouns as the Hebrew pairs them. 'For as long as the earth lasts' keeps כָּל־יְמֵי הָאָרֶץ, which Ibn Ezra reads as showing that the earth has an appointed end.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: the six seasons are two months each, as the sages taught: half Tishri, Marheshvan and half Kislev is זרע, half Kislev, Tevet and half Shevat is קֹר (חֹרֶף) (Bava Metzia 106). The English keeps the six nouns.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on קור: it is more severe than חֹרֶף.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on חרף: the time of sowing barley and legumes, which are 'sharp' (חֲרִיפִין) and ripen quickly; it is half Shevat, Adar and half Nisan. The English 'winter' is the nearest ordinary season.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on קציר: half Nisan, Iyar and half Sivan.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on קיץ: half Sivan, Tammuz and half Av, the time of gathering figs and drying them in the fields, hence the name קַיִץ as in 2 Sam 16:2.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on חום: the end of the days of heat, half Av, Elul and half Tishri, when the world is hottest.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'day and night shall not cease' implies that they had ceased during the days of the flood, since the constellations did not serve and day was not distinguished from night. The English does not state this.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they shall not cease from keeping their order. The English 'will never cease' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'all the days of the earth' is a sign that the earth has a fixed end; he adds a remark on the midrash 'round about eighteen thousand'. The English 'as long as the earth lasts' keeps the sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: He divided the year into two and afterwards into four; 'cold' is set against 'heat'. The English keeps the pairs.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'summer' is set against 'winter', and they correspond to the four seasons of the year; all of them divide day and night, so that what one lacks is added to the other. The English keeps the pairs.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak reports Ibn Ezra that 'all the days of the earth' shows it has an appointed end.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the year is divided into two parts, sowing and harvest, and then into four seasons.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: they ceased in the flood year; also seed and harvest, cold, heat, summer, winter and day and night ceased for those in the ark, as no distinction was made; the sages differ on whether the constellations served.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos translates word for word.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: 'will not cease' to continue in the unnatural manner that He set for them after the flood, because the sun now moves on a tilted wheel; before the flood it was always spring.

Grammar:

- וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם וְחִתְּכֶם is a pair of near synonyms, 'fear' and 'dread'. The suffix -כֶם is objective: the fear felt of you, not the fear you feel.
- The mahpakh on וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם is conjunctive and joins the two nouns; the pashta on וְחִתְּכֶם and the zaqef on יִהְיֶה are disjunctive and close the subject and then the verb.
- בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תִּרְמֹשׂ הָאֲדָמָה: the verb is feminine. Ibn Ezra gives two readings: 'on the ground' (the English), with an unstated feminine subject, or 'the ground' as the subject itself.
- נִתָּנוּ is a Niphal perfect: the creatures have been given into human hands.

Note: בְּכֹל is rendered 'upon' in step with the preceding עַל. Ibn Ezra offers two ways to take הָאֲדָמָה (place, or acting subject) and prefers to join בְּכֹל to מוֹרַאֲכֶם; the English takes the place sense and keeps the ordinary clause order.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וְחִתְּכֶם is 'your terror', like תִּרְאוּ חֲתַת (Job 6:21); the aggadah reads it as living, so the fear lasts only while you live.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: a doubled-root form from the root of תִּרְאוּ חֲתַת, the same as חִתָּתְכֶם.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the sense is 'on the ground', or else the ground is itself the acting subject; the English takes the first.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: כִּי בְיֶדְכֶם, 'for into your hand': the clause gives the reason for the fear, since the creatures have been given into your hand. The English joins it with a semicolon and leaves the causal link unstated.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: some say the bet of בְכֹל and וּבְכָל stands in place of a vav ('and'); the nearer reading is that it joins with מוֹרַאֲכֶם: the fear of you shall be on all that creeps and on all the fish. The English, with 'upon', takes this nearer reading.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'and the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon all beasts of the earth ...' reads the verse closely.

- The etnaḥta on אֶדְרְשֶׁנּוּ divides the verse: the first half states the demand for your blood and names the animal; the second names the human and narrows to 'each man ... his brother'.
- מִיַּד means 'from the hand of', an idiom for 'from, at the hands of'.

Note: The English keeps the sense Ibn Ezra gives (any blood of yours is not permitted; I will require it) rather than Rashi's limit to suicide. מִיַּד אִישׁ אָחִיו is rendered 'from each man for his brother', leaving 'brother' as a fellow human.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: though I permitted the taking of an animal's life, I will require your blood from the one who sheds his own.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: this includes the one who strangles himself, even though no blood came out.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: because the generation of the flood sinned and were left to wild beasts, it was needful to warn the animals about them (Psalm 49).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: from the one who kills deliberately where there are no witnesses, I will demand it.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: this speaks of a man who loved him as a brother and killed him by accident; I will demand an accounting if he does not confess and seek forgiveness, since even unintended killing needs atonement.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'I have permitted you to shed the blood of every living thing except your blood, the blood of your persons, for you are human: that I have not permitted, but I will require it.' Then he spells it out: from the human, whether many kill one or one kills one; and from every animal, in that I will command another animal to kill it, for the animals are permitted to you, not you to them. He calls the reading of 'your blood for your lives' as one who kills himself forced, and adds that v. 6 may be a command to the sons of Noah to kill the killer, which he calls right.

- The participle שֹׁפֵךְ opens a casus pendens, resumed by דָּמוֹ.
- בָּאָדָם can mean 'by a human (agent)' or 'for the sake of the human'.
- The clause כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם gives the ground for the penalty. It is a verbal clause: בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים is fronted before עָשָׂה, whose subject is not named (Rashi: 'the Maker').

Note: The English follows decisions (the human, with the article). 'By the human' is the plain agent reading; the other readings are kept in the commentary entries.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: if there are witnesses, you put him to death; why? because in the image of God ...
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the verse is elliptical and should read עָשָׂה הָעוֹשֶׂה אֶת הָאָדָם, 'the Maker made the human' in the image of God; the subject is left unstated, as often in Scripture. The English supplies the unstated subject as 'He'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בָּאָדָם means through witnesses, or before the eyes of all, or for the sake of the human whose blood was shed; there are many such uses. The English 'by the human' takes the first, the agent reading, with Rashi ('if there are witnesses, you put him to death').

**As for you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm over the earth and multiply in it.**

- The independent pronoun וְאַתֶּם sets 'you' apart: for Ramban, from the other living creatures told to swarm and multiply in 8:17; the midrash Rashi cites sets the command beside the shedder of blood in v. 6.
- Four imperatives close the speech: פְּרוּ, רְבוּ, שִׁרְצוּ, רְבוּ.
- The etnaḥta on וּרְבוּ divides the verse into the repeated blessing and the new commands.
- שִׁרְצוּ is the verb used of swarming creatures in 1:20-21 and 8:17.

Note: Genesis 1:28 and 9:1 give the same words as a blessing; here they are in the form of a command.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: on the plain sense, the first (9:1) is a blessing and here a command; by midrash, the one who does not engage in procreation is likened to one who sheds blood (Yevamot 63b).

- לֵאמֹר (lamed + infinitive construct) is the standard introduction to quoted speech.

Apparatus:

- Radak allows that the sons were also prophets, or that Noah was told to tell them.

- הִנְנִי מֵקִים: הִנֵּה with a suffix plus a participle presents the act as happening now or about to happen ('I am establishing').

- זֶרַע is a collective singular: 'seed' means all descendants.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: in וְאֶת זַרְעֲכֶם, אֶת means 'with' (עם). The third אִתְּכֶם (the second one in 9:10) either refers to those that were with you, or is repeated for added clarity. The covenant God will establish is that no flesh will be cut off.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the ו adds to 'be fruitful and multiply': you attend to populating the world, and I too will ensure it is never cut off.

- Radak (records): Radak: the last clause also brings in the offspring of the animals, as 'your offspring after you' did for humans.

Grammar:

- זֹאת is feminine, while אוֹת is of both genders, as Ibn Ezra notes.
- בֵּין is repeated before each party, as the idiom for 'between X and Y' requires.
- אֲנִי נֹתֵן with a participle states the act in progress.
- לְדֹרֹת is written defectively (without a vav), a point Rashi draws a lesson from.

Note: First use of אוֹת in the story. 'Sign' because the commentators' sense is a mark of the covenant.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: לדרת is written defectively, since some generations needed no sign, being wholly righteous, such as the generation of Hezekiah and of Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai. A homiletic point that does not alter the English.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אוֹת is both masculine and feminine, so זֹאת (feminine) agrees with it.
- Radak (follows): Radak: God explains to Noah and his sons that this is the sign so that they will not fear a flood when he sends rain.

**I have now set my bow in the cloud, and it will become a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.**

Literal: [obj] bow-of-me I-gave in-the-cloud and-it-will-be for-sign-of covenant between-me and-between the-earth

Grammar:

- The object אֶת קַשְׁתִּי is placed first for emphasis; נָתַתִּי is a perfect.
- קַשְׁתִּי 'my bow' has the suffix of God, a word picture that the commentators discuss.
- וְהָיְתָה לְ is the idiom 'it shall become'.
- בֵּינִי וּבֵין הָאָרֶץ: the earth, not only the people, is a party; verse 12 had 'every living creature'.

Note: The perfect נָתַתִּי is a point on which the commentators divide: Ibn Ezra says the bow is newly set now; Radak records Saadya, for whom it was set in nature at creation and is now made a sign. The English follows Ibn Ezra.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'I have now set a bow in the cloud'; the verse does not mean, as the Gaon said, that it existed at first.
- Radak (records): Radak: the bow arises from the sun's rays against the cloud after rain; God strengthened the sun's light after the flood, as Ibn Ezra writes in the name of a Gaon.
- Radak (records): Radak, reporting Saadya: נָתַתִּי has its plain meaning of the past: the bow set in nature in the cloud will be a sign for you, though it was not seen during the flood.

Apparatus:

- Ramban (on 9:12) argues the bow was in nature from creation.

- וְהָיָה ... וְנִרְאֲתָה: two weqatals; 'and it will be (when) ... and it will be seen'.
- בְּעַנְנִי עָנָן pairs a denominative verb with its cognate noun, which Radak takes as strengthening the action.
- The first nun is light (no dagesh), though the piel calls for one, as Ibn Ezra and Radak note.
- The nifal נִרְאֲתָה with the bow as subject means 'appear' or 'be seen'; Radak adds 'to humans'.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'when it comes up in my thought to bring darkness and destruction on the world'; the English keeps the plain sense of clouds.

- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: if we believed the Greek sages that the bow arises from the sun's heat, we could say God strengthened the sun's light after the flood. The comment is about the natural cause and does not change the English.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'I will cloud' by the intermediate causes that I have ordained.

- Radak (follows): Radak: the Torah speaks in human language; there is no forgetfulness before the throne of glory, so 'I will remember' is figurative.

Note: The English keeps 'God' in the third person, as the Hebrew does. Rashi's midrash (the attribute of justice above) is recorded, not adopted. Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'between' God's attribute of justice above and you; the text should say 'between me and', so the verse teaches that when the attribute of justice comes to accuse, God sees the sign and remembers. The English keeps the plain third person 'God'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'the bow will be in the cloud, which is for ever' means it is there in secret, and God sees it; the English says only that the bow will be in the cloud and God will see it.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'between God' is as if he said 'between me', as elsewhere (Exodus 24:1).
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos renders 'between the Memra of the LORD', avoiding the direct statement; it does not alter the sense of the Hebrew.

Apparatus:

- 9:16.1 וְהָיְתָה: feminine verb with the feminine noun קֶשֶׁת; no variant in the pack.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: God showed him the bow and said, 'This is the sign I spoke of'; the English 'This' points to the bow.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'This is the covenant I told you of, and this is the oath that I have established'; the English keeps the plain sense that the sign belongs to the established covenant.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: this is the third speech to Noah on the matter, to strengthen him; the Midrash counts six covenants against the six days of creation.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: the second bow is the sign, and Noah is to rouse the people to repent when it appears; homiletic.

- הַיֹּצְאִים is a participle with the article, 'those who came out'; the participle describes a completed event.
- וְחָם הוּא אֲבִי כְנָעַן is a nominal clause with a pronoun copula, opening a new thought; the etnaḥta on וָיָפֶת marks a break after the list.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the remark is needed here because the section is about Noah's drunkenness, in which Ham did wrong and Canaan was cursed; Ham's descendants have not yet been listed, so we would not know Canaan was his son.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: it teaches that both were evil, and why Canaan and not Cush is named: the section shows that the Canaanites are cursed; a homiletic and historical remark that does not change the words.
- Radak (follows): Radak: this is said for the story that follows about Noah and the wine.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: Ham resembled the notorious Canaan in his ways; a moral reading of 'father'.

#### Genesis 9:20

> וַיָּ֥חֶל נֹ֖חַ אִ֣ישׁ הָֽאֲדָמָ֑ה וַיִּטַּ֖ע כָּֽרֶם׃

**Noah, a man of the soil, began and planted a vineyard.**

Literal: and-began Noah man-of the-soil and-planted vineyard

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיָּ֥חֶל | and began — Hiphil wayyiqtol of חלל; Ibn Ezra derives it from the doubled root, Hiphil, 'begin' | ו: and + חָלַל | חלל | conjunction + verb (hifil, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 2 |
| נֹ֖חַ | Noah | נֹחַ | נוח | noun (proper name) |  |
| אִ֣ישׁ | man of — construct state; see note on 'man of the soil' | אִישׁ | אישׁ | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) |  |
| הָֽאֲדָמָ֑ה | the soil | ה: the + אֲדָמָה | אדם | particle (definite article) + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| וַיִּטַּ֖ע | and planted | ו: and + נָטַע | נטע | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| כָּֽרֶם׃ | vineyard | כֶּרֶם | כרם | noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- וַיָּחֶל is a Hiphil wayyiqtol of חלל, 'begin' (BDB Hiph 2); the same root in the Niphal and Piel means 'profane', which gives the wordplay Rashi uses.
- Two wayyiqtol verbs in a row, 'began' and 'planted', mean 'began to plant' (Radak).
- אִישׁ הָאֲדָמָה is a construct chain: 'man of the soil', a farmer.
- The etnaḥta on הָאֲדָמָה separates the description of Noah from the planting.

Note: The English keeps both verbs, 'began and planted', since the Hebrew does; the reading 'began to plant' is Radak's. Rashi's reading of וַיָּחֶל as 'made himself profane' (חֻלִּין), because he should have planted something else first, is recorded, not adopted. 'Man of the soil' is read as an expert farmer (Ibn Ezra), not 'master of the soil' (Rashi), a reading Ramban rejects.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'he made himself profane' (ḥullin), for he should first have planted something else (Genesis Rabbah).
- Rashi (records): Rashi: אִישׁ הָאֲדָמָה means 'master of the soil' (אֲדוֹנֵי הָאֲדָמָה), as אִישׁ נָעֳמִי (Ruth 1:3) means Naomi's husband. The English reads 'man of the soil' as a farmer.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: when he entered the ark he took shoots and fig cuttings with him (Genesis Rabbah); a midrashic note on the source of the vine.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיָּחֶל comes from the sense of 'beginning' (תְּחִלָּה). It is one of the doubled-root verbs, in the heavy augmented stem (the Hiphil), formed like וַיָּסֶךְ in 'who shut in the sea with doors' (Job 38:8). So it means 'began'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: he knew the work of the soil, a great skill; the midrash that he drank the wine the day he planted has a hidden meaning and is not the plain sense.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'began to plant and planted': the infinitive is joined with the word of beginning, as in 1 Samuel 14:35 and Deuteronomy 2:25.

#### Genesis 9:21

> וַיֵּ֥שְׁתְּ מִן־הַיַּ֖יִן וַיִּשְׁכָּ֑ר וַיִּתְגַּ֖ל בְּת֥וֹךְ אׇהֳלֹֽה׃

**He drank some of the wine, became drunk, and uncovered himself inside his tent.**

Literal: and-drank from-the-wine and-became-drunk and-uncovered-himself in-midst-of his-tent

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיֵּ֥שְׁתְּ | and drank — wayyiqtol of שׁתה; the BDB entry in the pack lists only the Niphal, so no sense is cited | ו: and + שָׁתָה | שׁתה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| מִן | from — partitive: 'some of' | מִן־ |  | preposition | 1.a |
| הַיַּ֖יִן | the wine | ה: the + יַ֫יִן | יין | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| וַיִּשְׁכָּ֑ר | and became drunk — ingressive: 'became drunk' | ו: and + שָׁכַר | שׁכר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal |
| וַיִּתְגַּ֖ל | and uncovered himself — Hitpael wayyiqtol of גלה, in the short (apocopated) form. The full form יִתְגַּלֶּה loses its final ה, and with it the doubling of the ל at the end of the word, which gives יִתְגַּל. The ת of the stem stays, before the ג. The sense is reflexive, 'uncovered himself'; the passive 'was uncovered' is also possible. | ו: and + גָּלָה | גלה | conjunction + verb (hitpael, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hithp 1 |
| בְּת֥וֹךְ | in the midst of — construct state | ב: in, with, by + תָּ֫וֶךְ |  | preposition + noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) |  |
| אׇהֳלֹֽה׃ | his tent — the final ה is the 3rd masculine suffix written ה instead of ו (the ketiv written אָהֳלֹה) | אֹ֫הֶל | אהל | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |

Grammar:

- Three wayyiqtol verbs narrate the sequence: וַיֵּשְׁתְּ 'drank', וַיִּשְׁכָּר 'became drunk', וַיִּתְגַּל 'uncovered himself'.
- וַיֵּשְׁתְּ and וַיִּתְגַּל are short (apocopated) wayyiqtol forms of verbs whose last root letter is ה; compare the full forms יִשְׁתֶּה and יִתְגַּלֶּה.
- וַיִּתְגַּל is a Hitpael of גלה: the ת of the stem is kept, and the doubled ל of the full form is simplified at the end of the word. The stem is reflexive (Ibn Ezra; Rashi 'לשון ויתפעל').
- אָהֳלֹה is spelled with a final ה where the pronominal suffix 'his' is normally written וֹ; the word means 'his tent'.
- The etnaḥta on וַיִּשְׁכָּר marks the break between the drinking and the exposure.

Note: 'Uncovered himself' is the reflexive reading; the passive 'was uncovered' (Radak: 'of himself', that is, without being forced) is the same sense. The spelling אהלה is read by Ibn Ezra and Radak as אָהֳלוֹ, ה for ו. Rashi's reading, a hint of the ten tribes called Oholah, is a midrash and is recorded, not adopted.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the form is the reflexive Hitpael ('לשון ויתפעל'); the English 'uncovered himself' reflects this.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: it is written אהלה, hinting at the ten tribes called after Samaria, called Oholah, who went into exile over wine (Amos 6); a midrashic reading.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: from the sense of 'uncovering', in the Hitpael, as in 'and he shall not lift himself up' (Jeremiah 51:3).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the ה of אהלה stands in place of the ו of the suffix 'his', as in בְּרֵעֹה 'in its shouting' (Exodus 32:17) and כִּי־פְרָעֹה 'for he had let them loose' (Exodus 32:25). So the English reads 'his tent'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: he drank without measure until he was drunk and disgraced.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'of himself': the uncovering was his own, not done by another.
- Radak (follows): Radak: it is written with ה, and many are like it, ה for ו; there is a midrash (Genesis Rabbah 36) on the ten tribes.

Apparatus:

- 9:21.7: the pack notes that WLC has abandoned or added a ketiv/qere relative to BHS here, agreeing with the Leningrad codex (L) against BHS; the text read is אָהֳלֹה.

- Radak (follows): Radak: Ham was the father of Canaan in that he did not cover his father's nakedness, a bad father of a bad son; he also told his brothers, mocking his father.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: Ham saw the disgrace that his son Canaan had done him, which was the castration, as some of the rabbis say.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: Ham told his brothers because he rejoiced at what his son had done.

| וּפְנֵיהֶם֙ | and their faces — construct plural 'faces of' with a suffix | ו: and + פָּנֶה | פנה | conjunction + noun (common, both genders, plural, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, plural) | I.1 |

| לֹ֥א | not | לֹא |  | particle (negative) |  |
| רָאֽוּ׃ | they saw — perfect (qatal) in a clause with a fronted object | רָאָה | ראה | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, common, plural) | Qal 1.a |

Grammar:

- וַיִּקַּח is singular though the subject is 'Shem and Japheth', so the verb agrees with the nearer name (Rashi finds a lesson in this); the next verb וַיָּשִׂימוּ is plural.
- עַל־שְׁכֶם שְׁנֵיהֶם is a construct chain with a singular noun: 'on the shoulder of the two of them'. Ibn Ezra explains the singular: each put part of the garment on his own shoulder.
- אֲחֹרַנִּית is an adverb, 'backwards'; it occurs twice, in the verb clause and in the verbless clause.
- וְעֶרְוַת אֲבִיהֶם לֹא רָאוּ puts the object first, for contrast with the covering.

Note: 'Both their shoulders' follows Ibn Ezra: each brother took part of the garment on his own shoulder. The repeated אֲחֹרַנִּית is kept; Rashi reads the second as the turning of their faces when they had to approach. Rashi's midrash on the singular וַיִּקַּח (Shem exerted himself more) is recorded, not adopted; Radak takes the singular as a plain idiom, like Exodus 6:10.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: it is not written 'they took' but 'he took', which teaches that Shem exerted himself more in the commandment than Japheth; hence his sons earned the fringed garment. The English does not adopt this.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: why is 'backward' said a second time? When they came near and had to turn to cover him, they turned their faces backward.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: each of them put part of the garment on his own shoulder. The word שְׁכֶם 'does not join' (לֹא תִתְחַבֵּר), that is, it is not put in the plural, so the singular serves for the two. So the English has 'both their shoulders'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'backward' means the reverse of the way a person goes, since all his motion is forward.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'Shem and Japheth took' is like 'Moses and Aaron came' (Exodus 6:10); they were quick to honour their father and covered him so as not to see him at all. The singular verb is an idiom.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: even in the act of covering, where they had to turn somewhat toward him, they did not, so as not to see, lest more grief be added to them.

#### Genesis 9:24

> וַיִּ֥יקֶץ נֹ֖חַ מִיֵּינ֑וֹ וַיֵּ֕דַע אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר־עָ֥שָׂה ל֖וֹ בְּנ֥וֹ הַקָּטָֽן׃

**Noah woke from his wine and learned what his youngest son had done to him.**

Literal: and-awoke Noah from-his-wine and-knew [obj] what-he-did to-him his-son the-small

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיִּ֥יקֶץ | and awoke — wayyiqtol of יקץ 'awake', a verb whose first root letter is yod: the prefix yod carries ḥireq and the root's yod is quiescent, written but not pronounced (Radak: וְיוֹ״ד הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ נֶעְלֶמֶת) | ו: and + יָקַץ | יקץ | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| נֹ֖חַ | Noah | נֹחַ | נוח | noun (proper name) |  |
| מִיֵּינ֑וֹ | from his wine — construct form יֵּינ- before the suffix | מ: from, than + יַ֫יִן | יין | preposition + noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| וַיֵּ֕דַע | and he learned — wayyiqtol: 'and he came to know' | ו: and + יָדַע | ידע | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1.c |
| אֵ֛ת | (object marker) | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| אֲשֶׁר | what | אֲשֶׁר | אשׁר | particle (relative) |  |
| עָ֥שָׂה | had done — perfect, here pluperfect in sense: the act precedes the waking | עָשָׂה | עשׂה | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal I.1 |
| ל֖וֹ | to him | ל: to, for |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| בְּנ֥וֹ | his son — construct with suffix | בֵּן |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |
| הַקָּטָֽן׃ | the youngest — הַקָּטָן: 'the small one', youngest, lesser or despised; see note | ה: the + קָטָן | קטן | particle (definite article) + adjective (adjective, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- וַיִּיקֶץ and וַיֵּדַע are wayyiqtols that carry the narrative on from the drunkenness of 9:21.
- אֵת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה is an object marker with a relative clause: 'what he had done'.
- הַקָּטָן is an adjective with the article after a noun with a suffix, so the pair is definite: 'his small son'.
- The etnaḥta after מִיֵּינוֹ divides the verse into the waking and the knowing.

Note: הַקָּטָן is ambiguous: 'small', so 'youngest', or 'lesser, despised'. Ibn Ezra reads בְּנוֹ הַקָּטָן as Canaan, the youngest of Ham's sons (10:6), the suffix of בְּנוֹ referring to Ham; the English 'his youngest son' follows him and leaves 'his' open. Rashi reads הַקָּטָן as 'the unfit and despised' (Jeremiah 49:15), not of age; in his reading (see his comment on 9:25) the son is Ham. Radak, if the son is Ham, also takes הַקָּטָן as 'the lesser', since Ham was not the youngest. The text does not say what was done (Ibn Ezra).

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: בנו הקטן means the unfit and despised one, as in 'Behold, I have made you small among the nations, despised among men' (Jeremiah 49:15). The English keeps the plain sense 'youngest' and records this.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Scripture does not reveal what was done; the doer was Canaan, since Ham saw and did not cover him as his brothers did but made the matter known, and Canaan heard. The English leaves the deed unstated.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'his youngest son' testifies that it was Canaan, for Scripture lists 'the sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan' (10:6); the suffix ו of בְּנוֹ refers back to Ham, mentioned before, and that is why Noah cursed Canaan. To say that Noah cursed his grandson because God had blessed his sons is the way of derash. The English 'his youngest son' leaves room for this reading.
- Radak (records): Radak: if it is said of Ham, הקטן means the lesser, since Ham was not young in years; the Sages explain that Canaan saw first or that Canaan castrated him.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: grandsons count as sons; Canaan was the smallest of Ham's sons, or smallest of Noah's grandsons, and also lowly among the nations.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: בריה זעירא 'his younger son'.

#### Genesis 9:25

> וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אָר֣וּר כְּנָ֑עַן עֶ֥בֶד עֲבָדִ֖ים יִֽהְיֶ֥ה לְאֶחָֽיו׃

**He said, "Cursed be Canaan; a slave among slaves shall he be to his brothers."**

Literal: and-said cursed Canaan slave-of slaves he-will-be to-his-brothers

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיֹּ֖אמֶר | and he said — wayyiqtol | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| אָר֣וּר | cursed — passive participle in a verbless curse formula: 'cursed be' | אָרַר | ארר | verb (qal, participle passive, masculine, singular, absolute) | Qal |
| כְּנָ֑עַן | Canaan | כְּנַ֫עַן |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| עֶ֥בֶד | slave of — construct before an indefinite plural: 'a slave of the class of slaves', one slave among them (Ibn Ezra); with the article, עֶבֶד הָעֲבָדִים, it would mean 'slave of the slaves' | עֶ֫בֶד | עבד | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 1 |
| עֲבָדִ֖ים | slaves | עֶ֫בֶד | עבד | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 1 |
| יִֽהְיֶ֥ה | he shall be — imperfect; with the jussive-like force of a curse | הָיָה | היה | verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal II.2 |
| לְאֶחָֽיו׃ | to his brothers — preposition ל with construct plural and suffix | ל: to, for + אָח | אחה | preposition + noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |

Grammar:

- אָרוּר כְּנַעַן is a verbless curse: passive participle then the subject.
- עֶבֶד עֲבָדִים is a construct chain of the same noun without the article. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'a slave like one of the slaves'; with the article it would mean 'slave of the slaves', as קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים (Exodus 26:33) differs from קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים (Leviticus 6:18).
- יִהְיֶה is imperfect, not the short jussive יְהִי, but in a curse the sense is a wish or decree.
- The etnaḥta under כְּנָעַן divides the curse from its content.

Note: The English 'a slave among slaves' follows Ibn Ezra, the normative commentator on these words: עֶבֶד עֲבָדִים means 'a slave like one of the slaves'; 'slave of the slaves' would need the article. Radak reads 'slave to slaves': his brothers will be slaves too and he a slave to them, the more so to the sons of Shem and Japheth; Sforno reads a degree of servitude added for his sin. For לְאֶחָיו Ibn Ezra names Cush, Egypt and Put, Ham's sons; Rashi has Canaan serve the seed of Shem and Japheth.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: Noah says to Ham, 'You caused me not to father another, fourth son to serve me; cursed be your fourth son, to serve the seed of these elder ones (Shem and Japheth), on whom the burden of serving me now falls.' And what led Ham to castrate him? He told his brothers that Adam had two sons and one killed the other for the inheritance of the world, and our father has three and still seeks a fourth. 'His brothers' are then Shem and Japheth; the English 'his brothers' leaves this open.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: עֶבֶד עֲבָדִים means a slave like one of the slaves; had it been עֶבֶד הָעֲבָדִים, with the article, it would mean a slave to slaves. The proof is קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים (Leviticus 6:18) beside בְּקֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים (Exodus 26:33). The English 'a slave among slaves' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: לאחיו means Cush, Egypt and Put, the sons of Ham; the view that Cushites are slaves because of Noah's curse of Ham is mistaken, since the first king after the flood was from Cush (10:10). The English 'his brothers' stays literal.
- Radak (records): Radak: his brothers too will be slaves, and he will be slave to them, all the more to the sons of Shem and Japheth.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: ליט כנען עבד פלח עבדין יהי לאחוהי.

#### Genesis 9:26

> וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בָּר֥וּךְ יְהֹוָ֖ה אֱלֹ֣הֵי שֵׁ֑ם וִיהִ֥י כְנַ֖עַן עֶ֥בֶד לָֽמוֹ׃

**He said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem, and may Canaan be a slave to them."**

Literal: and-said blessed the-LORD God-of Shem and-let-be Canaan slave to-them

| יְהֹוָ֖ה | the LORD | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |
| אֱלֹ֣הֵי | God of — construct plural form used for the one God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) | 2.d |
| שֵׁ֑ם | Shem | שֵׁם |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| וִיהִ֥י | and let be — jussive, short form וִיהִי | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, jussive, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal II.2 |
| כְנַ֖עַן | Canaan | כְּנַ֫עַן |  | noun (proper name) |  |
