Grammar:

- בָּרוּךְ יְהֹוָה is a verbless blessing formula; the passive participle precedes the subject.
- אֱלֹהֵי שֵׁם: the construct of אֱלֹהִים is plural in form but governs a singular sense.
- וִיהִי is a jussive, so 'may he be'; the wish repeats in 9:27.
- לָמוֹ is a poetic form of the plural suffix: 'to them'.

Note: לָמוֹ is ambiguous. Ibn Ezra reads 'to them' as God and Shem: Canaan will be a slave to Him and to Shem, compelled to serve; Sforno likewise, to the God of Shem and to Shem's seed. Rashi and Radak take it as Shem's descendants. The English keeps 'to them' so that the antecedent stays open.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: God will keep His promise to Shem's seed, to give them the land of Canaan. The English keeps the blessing of the LORD as God of Shem.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וִיהִי means that Canaan will be a tribute-paying servant to them, that is, Shem's descendants. The English 'to them' leaves the antecedent open.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: we must add thanks to God who is God of Shem and who will make Canaan a slave to Him and to Shem, who will compel him to serve; למו is like להם, with the ו added as in תביאמו (Exodus 15:17). The English 'to them' remains open.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: reports Ibn Ezra's reading, that Canaan is to be a slave to God and Shem, compelled to serve God, and Ibn Ezra's other explanation that he serves Japheth and Shem.
- Radak (follows): Radak: לָמוֹ means to the seed of Shem.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: a slave to the God of Shem and Shem's seed, as in Joshua 9:27, hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar of the LORD.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: וַאֲמַר בְּרִיךְ יְיָ אֱלָהֵהּ דְּשֵׁם וִיהֵי כְנַעַן עַבְדָא לְהוֹן.

#### Genesis 9:27

> יַ֤פְתְּ אֱלֹהִים֙ לְיֶ֔פֶת וְיִשְׁכֹּ֖ן בְּאׇֽהֳלֵי־שֵׁ֑ם וִיהִ֥י כְנַ֖עַן עֶ֥בֶד לָֽמוֹ׃

**May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem; and may Canaan be a slave to them.**

Literal: may-he-enlarge God to-Japheth and-let-dwell in-tents-of Shem and-let-be Canaan slave to-them

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| יַ֤פְתְּ | may he enlarge — hifil jussive of פתה with a wordplay on יֶפֶת | פָּתָה | פתה | verb (hifil, jussive, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph |
| אֱלֹהִים֙ | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| לְיֶ֔פֶת | Japheth | ל: to, for + יֶ֫פֶת |  | preposition + noun (proper name) |  |
| וְיִשְׁכֹּ֖ן | and may he dwell — jussive; the subject is God, carried over from the first wish (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak; Onkelos 'may He make His Presence dwell') | ו: and + שָׁכַן | שׁכן | conjunction + verb (qal, jussive, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 2 |
| בְּאׇֽהֳלֵי | in the tents of — construct plural | ב: in, with, by + אֹ֫הֶל | אהל | preposition + noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) | 1 |
| שֵׁ֑ם | Shem | שֵׁם |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| וִיהִ֥י | and may be — jussive | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, jussive, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal II.2 |

Grammar:

- יַפְתְּ is a hifil jussive of פתה, 'make wide', shortened from יַפְתֶּה: the final ה falls away and the word ends in two consonants, with dagesh lene in the ת, as in יַרְדְּ (Isaiah 41:2, cited by Ibn Ezra and Radak). The verb plays on the name יֶפֶת.
- The Hebrew has no object marker after אֱלֹהִים; the preposition ל marks Japheth: 'make wide for Japheth'.
- The pashta and zaqef qaton set אֱלֹהִים apart as the subject of the first wish.
- The refrain וִיהִי כְנַעַן עֶבֶד לָמוֹ repeats 9:26 word for word.

Note: The subject of וְיִשְׁכֹּן is not named. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak agree that it is God, who will dwell in the tents of Shem (Rashi: rest His Presence on Israel), and Onkelos renders 'may He make His Presence dwell'; the English 'he' continues the subject of the first wish, God. Rashi's midrash: though Cyrus, a descendant of Japheth, built the Second Temple, the Presence rested only in the First, built by Solomon of Shem. Sforno reads the tents of Shem as houses of study.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the Targum renders יַפְתֵּי, 'may He enlarge'. The English follows this sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: He (God) will rest His Presence on Israel. The Sages' midrash: although God enlarged Japheth, for Cyrus, of Japheth's line, built the Second Temple, the Presence did not rest in it; it rested in the First Temple, built by Solomon of Shem's line. The English 'he' takes God as the subject.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: even after the sons of Shem go into exile, slaves from Canaan's sons will be sold to them. The English 'a slave to them' fits.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יפת comes from יפה but means 'may He enlarge', like Deuteronomy 12:20, as in Aramaic, a hifil like 'and kings He subdues' (Isaiah 41:2); in this verse God blesses Japheth and Shem, since 'dwell in the tents of Shem' means God dwells in them, for the first verse blessed God. The English 'enlarge' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Canaan will be a slave to Shem and Japheth and to his brothers as well; so he is a slave to the world, since from these the whole earth was spread out; and this came about many years after the flood.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the Targum translates 'enlarge'; the root is פתה in the hifil, as in 'and kings He subdues' (Isaiah 41:2); God will enlarge Japheth's border and blessing, but His dwelling will be only in the tents of Shem, an allusion to Israel.
- Radak (follows): Radak: Canaan will also be a slave to the sons of Japheth.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: the tents of Shem are houses of study, apart from the Temple.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: the second servitude is to Shem and Japheth, also outside the time of the Temple.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: יַפְתֵּי יְיָ לְיֶפֶת וְיַשְׁרֵי שְׁכִינְתֵּיהּ בְּמַשְׁכְּנֵיהּ דְּשֵׁם.

- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: do not seek a meaning for every name; this does not bear on the English.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'he began to show the mighty deeds of men over the animals, for he was a mighty hunter'. The English follows this.

**He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; therefore it is said, Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD.**

Literal: he-was mighty-of hunting before the-LORD on-so it-is-said like-Nimrod mighty-of hunting before the-LORD

Grammar:

- גִּבֹּר־צַיִד is a construct chain: 'mighty one of hunting'.
- יֵאָמַר is nifal imperfect: 'it will be said', a proverbial formula, here with the saying quoted after כְּ.
- The etnaḥta on יְהוָה divides the verse into the statement about Nimrod and the proverb it explains.
- The saying repeats the first half, with כְּנִמְרֹד replacing הוּא הָיָה.

Note: The Hebrew leaves the sense of לִפְנֵי יהוה open. The English keeps the words and does not choose. Rashi reads it as defiance: Nimrod trapped people's minds with his words and led them to rebel, and 'before the LORD' means he meant to provoke Him to His face. Ibn Ezra, calling his reading the plain sense, takes it that he built altars and offered the game as burnt offerings to God. Radak and Sforno read it as an intensifier ('exceedingly mighty'). Ramban quotes Rashi and the Sages and rejects Ibn Ezra, but his own reading is that Nimrod was the first to rule over men by force, a hunter of beasts as well, with 'before the LORD' as hyperbole: none under heaven was his equal in might. Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that 'it is said' introduces a proverb.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: צָד דַּעְתָּן שֶׁל בְּרִיוֹת בְּפִיו, he trapped people's minds with his speech and led them to rebel against God; so the hunting is figurative. The English says only 'hunter'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: מִתְכַּוֵן לְהַקְנִיטוֹ עַל פָּנָיו, he intended to provoke Him to His face. The English keeps 'before the LORD' without choosing this sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: of any man who is brazenly wicked, knowing his Master and intending to rebel against Him, people will say 'like Nimrod, a mighty hunter'. The English follows him in taking the verb as a proverb formula.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the sense of לפני ד' is that he built altars and offered the animals up as burnt offerings to God (עולה לשם, 'to the Name'); this is the way of the plain sense (דרך הפשט), and the midrash goes another way. Recorded as an alternative.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מָשָׁל הָיָה גַם בִּימֵי משה, it was a proverb even in Moses' time. The English follows in presenting the clause as a saying.
- Radak (records): Radak: לפני ה' magnifies the might, as in 'a great city to God' (Jonah 3:3); the English does not adopt this.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: 'very mighty', like עיר גדולה לאלהים; recorded as the intensifier reading.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders גִּבֹּר צַיִד as גִּבַּר תַּקִּיף, 'a mighty man', with no word for hunting, and לִפְנֵי יְהוָה as קֳדָם יְיָ, 'before the LORD'. Radak takes this rendering as support for his reading of the verse as praise of Nimrod's might.

Grammar:

- מִן־הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא is placed before the verb, so the departure from Shinar is emphasised.
- אַשּׁוּר is a personal name here (the subject of וַיִּבֶן), though it is also the name of the land.
- Each city is marked with אֶת; the repeated אֶת־ divides the list.
- The merkha on רְחֹבֹת and tipḥa on עִיר show the two words are read together.

Note: אַשּׁוּר may be read as the land (to Asshur he went out, i.e. 'he went out to Assyria', Ramban). The English takes it as the person who went out, as Rashi and Ibn Ezra do. Whether עִיר is part of the name Rehoboth-Ir or means 'the wide streets of the city' (that is, of Nineveh) is left open. The final comma leaves the list to continue into verse 12.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: when Asshur saw his sons obey Nimrod and rebel against God by building the tower, he left their midst. The English follows in taking Asshur as the subject who went out from that land.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Asshur is a son of Japheth (sic, in the text as printed); this was after the division of the earth, and Nimrod was the first king over Babel. The English follows in taking Asshur as a person who left; Ramban's reading of the verb as 'Nimrod went out to Asshur' is not adopted.

Apparatus:

- Ramban takes Nimrod as the subject of 'went out' and אַשּׁוּר as his destination, 'he went out to Asshur', since Asshur was of the sons of Shem (10:22). He cites verbs of motion with a bare accusative of the goal, without ה of direction (Num 34:4; Deut 3:1), and Micah 5:5, which calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'. Radak takes Asshur as the subject, of Ham or of Shem.

- הִוא הָעִיר הַגְּדֹלָה is a verbless clause; the feminine pronoun agrees with עִיר.

Note: The antecedent of הִוא is ambiguous. Rashi takes it as Nineveh, citing Jonah 3:3; Ibn Ezra prefers Nineveh and allows Resen or Calah. Radak, against 'most commentators', takes it as Resen. The English keeps the pronoun as 'that' and does not name the city; the reading of the normative commentators, Nineveh, is the one the edition takes.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: הִיא נִינְוֵה, as it says 'Nineveh was an exceedingly great city to God' (Jonah 3:3). The English leaves the antecedent open in wording, though agreeing with this reading.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the reading closest to his view is that the clause joins 'and he built Nineveh', so the great city is Nineveh; to join it to Resen or to Calah is not far-fetched either. The English leaves the pronoun open in its wording and allows his preferred reading.

Apparatus:

- Whether הִוא refers to Nineveh, Resen or the group Nineveh-Resen-Calah is disputed; Ibn Ezra allows Resen or Calah.

- All four names are plural gentilics in -ִים, so they name peoples, not single persons.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: these are names of countries, in each of which is a family, so all are plural; the proof is that the Philistines went out from there and שם refers to a place. The English follows by writing the names as plural peoples.

Apparatus:

- The BDB entry glosses נַפְתֻּחִים as 'the northern land' and כַּפְתֹּרִי as 'Cretans'; these are data from the lexicon, not decisions of the English.

Grammar:

- אֲשֶׁר ... מִשָּׁם is a relative clause with a resumptive adverb: 'which ... from there'.
- The relative clause may attach to Pathrusim and Casluhim together or only to the second; the revia on כַּסְלֻחִים closes the pair.
- The Philistines follow the verb as subject: 'went out from there, the Philistines'.
- The verse ends the Mizraite list with Caphtorim, set after the parenthesis.

Note: The relative clause is ambiguous in attachment. Rashi takes it as 'from both', the Philistines coming from the Pathrusim and Casluhim together; the English leaves the antecedent as the pair. The Caphtorim stand after the parenthesis. Ibn Ezra says that Mizraim fathered the Caphtorim too, and explains why ילד is said of a father: the son comes from the father's vigour and strength, in his image and likeness.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: מִשְּׁנֵיהֶם יָצְאוּ, the Philistines came from both, since the Pathrusim and Casluhim exchanged their wives' beds. The English follows on the antecedent (both) but not on the explanation.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Egypt also fathered the Caphtorim, and because the son comes from the father's strength and likeness, one says 'fathered' of him. The English keeps 'and the Caphtorim' as a further object of fathered in verse 13.

Apparatus:

- The Philistines are named in the verse as coming from the Casluhim (Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 say Caphtor), a known difficulty; the English does not harmonize.

Grammar:

- בֹּאֲכָה is an infinitive construct of בוא with the long form of the 2nd person masculine singular suffix (-כָה for -ךָ), 'your coming'; it works as an idiom 'as you come to', 'in the direction of'.
- The directional he on גְרָרָה and סְדֹמָה means 'to Gerar', 'to Sodom'.
- The etnaḥta on עַזָּה divides the verse in two: the line from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, then the line toward Sodom and the cities with it as far as Lasha. Within each half the zaqef qaton and the gershayim mark lesser breaks.
- Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim are listed with a waw on each of the last three.

Note: בֹּאֲכָה, literally 'your coming', is rendered 'toward'. Ibn Ezra glosses בֹּאֲכָה גְרָרָה as אֶל גְּרָר, 'to Gerar'; Rashi takes the word as a verbal noun and explains it as a man telling his friend that the border reaches until you come to the border of a given place. The two readings agree, and the English follows both.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: גְּבוּל means the end of his land; every גְּבוּל means end and edge. The English 'border' follows this.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בֹּאֲכָה is a שֵׁם דָּבָר, a verbal noun ('your coming'). 'And it seems to me' it is like a man saying to his friend: this border reaches until you come to the border of so-and-so. The English 'toward' follows this.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בֹּאֲכָה גְרָרָה means 'to Gerar'. The English 'toward Gerar' follows.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the passage shows that God intended the Canaanites to settle the land until their end, for Israel's sake. This is theological, not about the words.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: וַהֲוָה תְּחוּם כְּנַעֲנָאֵי מִצִּידוֹן מָטֵי לִגְרָר עַד עַזָּה, 'reaching to Gerar'.
- Lasha is not identified with any known place in the pack.

Grammar:

- יֻלַּד is a Pual perfect 3ms with no stated subject; Radak says it is general, 'children were born'.
- גַּם־הוּא 'he also': the line resumes Shem after the sons of Ham and Japheth have been listed (Ramban).
- אֲבִי כָּל־בְּנֵי־עֵבֶר is a construct chain of four nouns, 'father-of all-of sons-of Eber': the first three are in the construct state and only עֵבֶר is absolute.
- הַגָּדוֹל after Japheth is ambiguous in the Hebrew: it can describe Japheth or Shem.
- The etnaḥta on הוּא divides the verse: the first half says that Shem had children; the second gives two titles of Shem, 'father of all the sons of Eber' and 'brother of Japheth the elder', set apart by the zaqef on עֵבֶר. Silluq closes the verse on הַגָּדוֹל.

Note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take 'the elder' to describe Japheth (Noah was five hundred when he began to beget and Shem was a hundred two years after the flood), so the English follows them. Ramban and Radak allow it to describe Shem; recorded in the apparatus. Eber is taken as the personal name, so 'sons of Eber' are his descendants. The pack gives sense Pu for יֻלַּד and no sense fits גָּדוֹל here ('elder' in age), so none is given.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: עֵבֶר here is '[beyond] the River' (עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר): Shem was the father of all who lived beyond the River. On this reading 'the sons of Eber' are the people of a region, not the descendants of the man Eber.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: I do not know whether 'the elder' is Japheth or Shem. Since Shem was a hundred years old two years after the flood and Noah was five hundred at the first birth, the eldest son was a hundred at the flood, so 'the elder' is Japheth.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'brother of Japheth' and not 'brother of Ham', because those two honored their father and Ham shamed him. This explains the choice of name, not the sense of the words.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'father of all the sons of Eber' makes Shem known as the father of the Hebrews: none stands above him, and the LORD is his God, as in 'the LORD, the God of the Hebrews' (Exod 10:3). Canaan is the father of those below whom there is none, and holy is not to be mixed with profane.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Japheth is the elder, and Scripture names Shem first out of respect. He shows the dates and records the view that Shem is the older.
- Ramban (records): Ramban prefers 'the elder' as describing Shem, the elder brother of Japheth, since Ham is the youngest though listed first.

Apparatus:

- עֵבֶר: the man Eber of 10:24-25, whose descendants are the Hebrews (Ibn Ezra), or the land beyond the River, עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר, whose people all descend from Shem (Rashi, Ramban).
- הַגָּדוֹל: Japheth the elder (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, most commentators) or Shem the elder brother of Japheth (Ramban, Radak, and some cited by Ibn Ezra).
- Onkelos: וּלְשֵׁם אִתְיְלִיד אַף הוּא ... אֲחוּהִי דְיֶפֶת רַבָּא, with the same ambiguity.

#### Genesis 10:25

> וּלְעֵ֥בֶר יֻלַּ֖ד שְׁנֵ֣י בָנִ֑ים שֵׁ֣ם הָֽאֶחָ֞ד פֶּ֗לֶג כִּ֤י בְיָמָיו֙ נִפְלְגָ֣ה הָאָ֔רֶץ וְשֵׁ֥ם אָחִ֖יו יׇקְטָֽן׃

Literal: and-to-Eber was-born two sons name-of the-one Peleg for in-days-his was-divided the-earth and-name-of brother-his Joktan

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וּלְעֵ֥בֶר | and to Eber | ו: and + ל: to, for + עֵ֫בֶר |  | conjunction + preposition + noun (proper name) |  |
| יֻלַּ֖ד | was born — Pual perfect 3ms; its subject is the plural שְׁנֵי בָנִים that follows: a verb placed before its subject may stay singular (Radak: 'in a general way', as in 41:50) | יָלַד | ילד | verb (pual, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Pu |
| שְׁנֵ֣י | two of | שְׁנַ֫יִם | שׁנה | adjective (cardinal number, masculine, dual, construct) |  |

| שֵׁ֣ם | the name of — construct state | שֵׁם |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 3 |

| כִּ֤י | for | כִּי |  | conjunction | 3 |
| בְיָמָיו֙ | in his days — plural construct with suffix | ב: in, with, by + יוֹם |  | preposition + noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 4 |
| נִפְלְגָ֣ה | was divided — Niphal perfect 3fs; the earth is feminine here | פָּלַג | פלג | verb (nifal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Niph |
| הָאָ֔רֶץ | the earth — the earth stands for its peoples: Rashi, they were scattered and divided over the whole world | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| וְשֵׁ֥ם | and the name of | ו: and + שֵׁם |  | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 3 |
| אָחִ֖יו | his brother | אָח | אחה | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |
| יׇקְטָֽן׃ | Joktan — 'small'; the text gives no reason for the name | יׇקְטָן |  | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- יֻלַּד is singular, but its subject is the plural שְׁנֵי בָנִים, which follows it: a verb placed before its subject may keep the singular (Radak: said 'in a general way').
- פֶּלֶג and נִפְלְגָה share the root פלג: a wordplay in the explanation of the name.
- The accents mark שֵׁם הָאֶחָד פֶּלֶג off from the 'for' clause.
- שֵׁם אָחִיו has no verb; the nominal clause runs on from the previous one.

Note: Rashi and Radak take 'the earth was divided' as the dispersion of the peoples. They differ on its time: Rashi, after Seder Olam, puts it at the end of Peleg's days, in the year of his death; Radak says that when Peleg was born the dispersion was already being prepared. Radak ties the shortening of lifespans to the name Joktan, Sforno to the dispersion; neither takes נִפְלְגָה itself to mean it. The English keeps the plain verb.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the languages were confused, and the people scattered from the valley and were divided over the whole world. Eber was a prophet, who named his son for what was to come. Seder Olam teaches that the division came at the end of Peleg's days: not at their start, for his younger brother Joktan had already fathered many families, and not in their middle, for Scripture would have said so; so it fell in the year Peleg died.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: Joktan was humble and made himself small, so he merited to raise all these families. This is a homily on the name.
- Radak (records): Radak: when Peleg was born the people were preparing for the dispersion, so he named him Peleg.
- Radak (records): Radak: no reason is given for Joktan; some say lifespans shrank from then, so the name means the smallness of years.

Apparatus:

- נִפְלְגָה: the division of the earth's peoples at the dispersion (Rashi, Radak, Sforno). Its time: at the end of Peleg's days, in the year of his death (Rashi, after Seder Olam), or already in preparation when he was born (Radak).

| הַ֥ר | mountain of — construct state | הַר | הרר | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 1 |
| הַקֶּֽדֶם׃ | the east | ה: the + קֶ֫דֶם | קדם | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1.b |

Grammar:

- וַיְהִי is a wayyiqtol of הָיָה, here 'was situated' with the singular verb before the subject מוֹשָׁבָם.
- בֹּאֲכָה is an infinitive construct with a 2nd person suffix: 'as you come'; with סְפָרָה (directional ה) the phrase means 'in the direction of Sephar'.
- הַר הַקֶּדֶם is a construct chain: 'the mountain of the east'.
- The etnaḥta on מִמֵּשָׁא divides the starting point from the boundary.

Note: Hebrew has no 'to' before הַר הַקֶּדֶם. It may stand in apposition to סְפָרָה ('Sephar, the eastern mountain'), or mark the second boundary. The English follows Radak and reads it as the end of the range.

Commentary:

- Radak (follows): Radak: after the division they chose the land from Mesha to הַר הַקֶּדֶם, the eastern mountain, and settled there. Saadia identifies מֵשָׁא with Mecca, where the Ishmaelites go on pilgrimage.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: וַהֲוָה מוֹתְבָנְהוֹן מִמֵּשָׁא מָטֵי לִסְפַר טוּר מָדִינְחָא, 'and their dwelling was from Mesha, reaching to Sephar, the mountain of the east'. He renders בֹּאֲכָה by מָטֵי 'reaching' and puts ל before סְפַר only, so טוּר מָדִינְחָא stands in apposition to Sephar as the one end point; the English, with Radak, takes the eastern mountain as the end of the range, and keeps his reading here.

Apparatus:

- The location of מֵשָׁא and סְפָר is uncertain; Saadia as quoted by Radak identifies מֵשָׁא with Mecca.

Grammar:

- אֵלֶּה בְנֵי־שֵׁם is a verbless clause: 'these (are) the sons of Shem'.
- Four phrases follow with the same pronominal suffix, each with a prefix: three with ל and one with ב.
- The zaqef on שֵׁם sets off the statement; the tipḥa and etnaḥta then divide the four categories in pairs.
- לָשׁוֹן, 'tongue', here has the sense 'language'. The table of nations already counts languages; the story of how the one language was confused follows in 11:1–9, where the word for 'language' is שָׂפָה.

Note: The same four-part formula closes Ham's line (10:20); here it closes Shem's.

Commentary:

- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos renders מִשְׁפְּחֹתָם by זַרְעֲיָתְהוֹן 'their families' and גּוֹיֵהֶם by עַמְמֵיהוֹן 'their peoples'; he puts ל before 'their lands' and ב before 'their peoples', the reverse of the Hebrew's בְּ and לְ, with no change of sense.

**These are the clans of the sons of Noah, by their lineages, in their nations; and from these the nations were divided on the earth after the flood.**

Grammar:

- Hebrew puts the verb before its subject: נִפְרְדוּ הַגּוֹיִם, 'were divided the nations'; the nifal gives a passive or reflexive sense.
- The etnaḥta on בְּגוֹיֵהֶם divides the verse: the first half closes the genealogy, the second (from וּמֵאֵלֶּה) looks beyond it to the spread of the nations. The geresh on וּמֵאֵלֶּה and the tevir on הַגּוֹיִם are lesser divisions within the second half.
- הַמַּבּוּל, 'the flood', is the word for the Flood of chapters 6 to 9; outside Genesis it occurs only in Psalm 29:10.
- פ at the end is a paragraph break (petuḥa), which closes the whole table of nations.

Note: The English keeps 'after the flood' as stated, attached to the dividing of the nations. Radak objects that the nations did not separate until after the dispersion (הַפַּלָּגָה) of Peleg's time (10:25), and so attaches 'after the flood' to the families: those born after the flood separated in the land when they separated, which was after the dispersion. His reading is recorded in the commentary.

Commentary:

- Radak (records): Radak: in fact they did not separate until after the dispersion (הַפַּלָּגָה, in Peleg's time), so the verse cannot mean that the separation came straight after the flood; 'rather its meaning is' (אֶלָּא פֵּרוּשׁוֹ), and his explanation follows in the next comment. The English keeps the plain order and records his reading.
- Radak (records): Radak: those born after the flood spread out over the earth when they spread out, which was after the Peleg division.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos translates 'and from these the peoples were separated in the earth after the flood', in line with the English.

Apparatus:

- Radak reads the dispersal as later than the flood by the interval of the Peleg division (10:25).

> וַיְהִ֥י כׇל־הָאָ֖רֶץ שָׂפָ֣ה אֶחָ֑ת וּדְבָרִ֖ים אֲחָדִֽים׃

**Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.**

Literal: and-was all-of the-earth language one and-words one(pl)

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |

| וַיְהִ֥י | and it was — wayyiqtol of הָיָה, 'it was / it came to be' | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III |
| כׇל | all of — construct state | כֹּל | כלל | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 1 |
| הָאָ֖רֶץ | the earth | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| שָׂפָ֣ה | language — שָׂפָה is literally 'lip'; here 'speech, language' | שָׂפָה | שׂפה | noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 2 |
| אֶחָ֑ת | one — pausal form of אַחַת under the etnaḥta: segol for pataḥ under the alef | אֶחָד | אחד | adjective (cardinal number, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| וּדְבָרִ֖ים | and words | ו: and + דָּבָר | דבר | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | III |
| אֲחָדִֽים׃ | the same (lit. 'one') — plural of 'one'; 'one and the same', 'identical' | אֶחָד | אחד | adjective (cardinal number, masculine, plural, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- וַיְהִי with a subject and a following predicate (שָׂפָה אֶחָת) states a condition: 'the whole earth was of one language'.
- כָל־הָאָרֶץ is the whole earth by metonymy for all its people (Radak: כָּל בְּנֵי הָאָרֶץ).
- אֲחָדִים is the plural of אֶחָד, rare; it agrees in gender with דְּבָרִים (masculine), while שָׂפָה takes the feminine אֶחָת.
- אֶחָת is the pausal form of אַחַת (segol for pataḥ) under the etnaḥta, which divides the verse: 'one language' // 'and the same words'.

Note: 'Language' is the sense of שָׂפָה here; 'lip' is the literal sense. אֲחָדִים is read as 'the same' (identical words), the sense Ibn Ezra gives (the words meant the same to all); Rashi's 'one counsel' is recorded as an alternative.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: שפה אחת means the holy tongue (Hebrew). The English says 'one language'; the identification is recorded here and in the apparatus.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: they came with one counsel and said, 'He has no right to choose the upper realms for Himself; let us go up to the firmament and make war with Him.' Another interpretation: their words were against the Only One of the world. Another: they said that once every 1656 years the firmament totters, as it did in the days of the flood, so let us make supports for it (Bereshit Rabbah). The English keeps the plain sense 'the same words', with Ibn Ezra.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אֶחָת has a small pataḥ (segol) under the alef when absolute, and a big pataḥ (pataḥ) when in construct (אַחַת). The dispersion was about a hundred years after the flood, and Peleg was named for it; following Seder Olam, Abraham was among the builders, with Noah and Shem still alive. 'One language' means one tongue, most likely the holy tongue, as the names Adam, Eve, Cain, Seth and Peleg witness.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אֲחָדִים means that today words in every language are not understood by all speakers of it, but then the sayings of the wise and the foolish were 'the same'; the plural אחדים is from אֶחָד.

Apparatus:

- Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak identify the one language with the holy tongue; Onkelos has 'one tongue and one speech'.
- Radak (11:1:3) takes 'one words' as one agreement (cf. Joshua 9:2 'with one mouth').

Grammar:

- וַיְהִי בְּ + infinitive construct is the regular way to say 'it was when ...'; the main clause follows with wayyiqtol (וַיִּמְצְאוּ).
- בְּנָסְעָם: root נסע with the preposition בְּ and a plural suffix, 'in their setting out'.
- The wayyiqtols וַיִּמְצְאוּ and וַיֵּשְׁבוּ carry the narrative forward.
- The etnaḥta on מִקֶּדֶם separates the journey from the finding.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they had been dwelling at 'the mountain of the east' (10:30) and set out from there to find a place that would hold them all, and found only Shinar. The English 'from the east' follows him.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the words 'as they set out from the east' are a sign that the mountains of Ararat are in the east.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וימצאו בקעה means they sought a good place to build a city until they found this plain; בקעה is a flat, level plain, opposite of 'rough places', though it may also lie between mountains as if cleft.
- Radak (follows): Radak: מקדם is from the east, where humanity first lived; the plain is level ground between mountains.

Apparatus:

- מִקֶּדֶם can also mean 'eastward' or 'of old' (lexicon senses 1.b and 2). Ramban rejects Rashi's link with 'the mountain of the east' (10:30): that verse speaks only of Shem's descendants, while Japheth's and Ham's were more numerous, and their settlement in their lands came after the dispersion. He agrees with Ibn Ezra that Ararat lies in the east, near Assyria, and that Noah's descendants moved from there to the plain.
- Onkelos translates 'in the beginning' (בְּקַדְמֵיתָא), taking קדם as 'of old', and 'land of Babylon' for שִׁנְעָר.

- הָבָה is the imperative of יָהַב ('give') with paragogic he, but it functions as an interjection ('come now'), and so can address women or a plural group (Radak, Ibn Ezra).
- נִלְבְּנָה לְבֵנִים and נִשְׂרְפָה לִשְׂרֵפָה pair a cohortative verb with a cognate noun; Radak compares 'and David fasted a fast'.
- The first clause of the second sentence (וַתְּהִי ... הַלְּבֵנָה לְאָבֶן) has verb first; the second (וְהַחֵמָר הָיָה ...) has subject first, giving the two a chiastic balance.
- אֶבֶן and לְבֵנָה, חֵמָר and חֹמֶר form two sound-pairs: stone/brick, bitumen/mortar.
- לְאָבֶן has qamets under the alef instead of segol (אֶבֶן): a pausal form under the zaqef qaton, as Radak notes (compare פָּרֶץ, Ruth 4:18; עָבֶד, Gen 44:17).

Note: חֵמָר is rendered 'bitumen' (the lexicon's sense); Ibn Ezra agrees (the word as in Arabic, used in place of clay). Radak takes חֵמָר as clay kneaded with water, recorded here. Rashi's remark that there are no stones in Babylon explains why brick stood for stone.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'a man to his fellow' means nation to nation, Egypt to Cush, Cush to Put, Put to Canaan. The English keeps the ordinary sense 'one to another'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: הבה is a call to prepare oneself, to join for work, for counsel or for a burden; 'come' conveys the summons.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they made bricks because there are no stones in Babylon, which is a plain.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: this is how bricks are made, burned in a kiln; the English 'burn them hard'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: לחמר is for plastering the wall; the English 'mortar'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: נִלְבְּנָה is from לְבֵנִים; although that plural ends in ־ים, the noun is feminine, like נָשִׁים and פִּילַגְשִׁים. They burned the bricks until they were hard: the strong building that neither water nor fire dissolves.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'the brick became for them stone' means 'instead of stone'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the bitumen served 'instead of clay' (תחת טיט), and the word means what it does in Arabic ('the language of Ishmael'), that is, bitumen; the English follows him. He adds that the builders were not fools who thought to climb to heaven, nor afraid of a flood, since Noah and his sons were with them, but meant to build a great city to live in and a tall tower as a sign, a name and a renown, so that those out with the flocks could find the city and their name would last as long as the tower stood.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Anchored here by the matching program: Ibn Ezra says not to be surprised by 'its top in the heavens' (11:4), since Moses speaks of 'cities great and fortified up to heaven' (Deut 1:28); the builders thought their plan secure, but the LORD did not counsel it. It bears on 11:4, not on 11:3.
- Radak (records): Radak: חֵמָר is clay kneaded with water; חֹמֶר is a mix of lime and sand; there was no stone to burn for lime, so they used חֵמָר instead.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos keeps חֵמָר as חֵימָרָא and renders לַחֹמֶר as לְשִׁיעַ ('for plaster'); for לְבֵנִים he has לִבְנִין, and for לִשְׂרֵפָה 'in fire' (בְּנוּרָא).

- The pashta on וּמִגְדָּל and the revia on עִיר divide the object phrase.

- Radak (follows): Radak: the city was for living in, the tower for watching their flocks from afar and as a landmark for the shepherds to find their way back.
- Radak (follows): Radak: וראשו בשמים means that the tower would be very high, as in 'cities great and fortified up to the heavens' (Deut 1:28), in height of the air.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: 'let us make a name' means an idol in the tower, so that its renown would make it the 'god of gods' and its king would rule all humanity.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders 'its top reaching to the heavens' (מָטֵי עַד צֵית שְׁמַיָּא), an interpretive extension; he translates שֵׁם as 'a name' (שׁוּם) and פֶּן as 'perhaps/lest' (דִּילְמָא).

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: all that happens below depends on the power of the heights, so God is called 'rider of the heavens'; the writer says 'came down' in the way human beings speak.
- Radak (follows): Radak: אשר בנו means 'which they began to build'.

- Radak on בנו: 'which they began to build'. Ibn Ezra on 11:8: they had built part of the city and the tower, or 'built' in their thoughts. Onkelos: 'the LORD revealed Himself to take vengeance on the deeds of the city and tower which the sons of men built'.

The English takes 'held back' from him but reads the clause as a statement, with Ibn Ezra; the question is recorded in the note.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: He said this to the angels, and that is the meaning of 'and came down' (יָרַד, 'He had gone down because He said so'). The English gives no addressee.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'one people' with one religion; when religions differ, jealousy and hatred arise, and also when languages differ, so the king of Persia commanded each to speak in his own language (Esth 1:22).
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the ה of הַחִלָּם is pointed with a big pataḥ (pataḥ) because of the ח after it, as in הַחִלֹּתִי (Deut 2:31). A point of vocalisation.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יִבָּצֵר is like יִמָּנַע, as in 'fortified (בצורות) cities' (Deut 3:5); the sense is, if I leave them they will think they can do whatever they wish.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יָזְמוּ has the sense of זָמְמוּ ('they planned'), but the two words are of two different roots.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'one people' means they have one agreement, as in 'we will become one people' (Gen 34:16).
- Sforno (records): Sforno: what undoes counsels and defeats plans is dissension over religions or languages; these were one in religion (following the astrologers) and one in language.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra, in his comment, reads 'and now not will it be withheld' conditionally: 'if I leave them alone'. Radak: 'if we do not annul them'.
- Onkelos: 'and now it will not be withheld from them, all that they have thought to do'.

Grammar:

- The cohortatives נֵרְדָה and נָבְלָה are plural (1st person), 'let us ...'; Rashi (and Radak) take the נ as the plural prefix and the final ה as the extra he like נֵרְדָה.
- The pack parses וְנָבְלָה as qal cohortative of בלל. Ibn Ezra argues against the grammarians who derive it from the nifal, and proposes a hifil (נָבֵלָה), which is in line with 'for there the LORD confused' (11:9).
- אֲשֶׁר לֹא is a final/result clause, 'so that not'; יִשְׁמְעוּ is 'hear' in the sense 'understand'.
- אִישׁ שְׂפַת רֵעֵהוּ is the idiom for 'each the language of the other'.

Note: 'Let us' keeps the plural of the Hebrew, whose addressees Rashi (His court) and Ibn Ezra (the angels) both take to be the heavenly company. The pack's data parse וְנָבְלָה as qal of בלל; Ibn Ezra's hifil is recorded, but the English 'confuse' fits both. The pack gives no qal sense for שָׁמַע, so none is cited.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: He consulted His court, out of His great humility; hence the plural 'let us'.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: measure for measure: they said 'let us build', He answered in kind with 'let us go down'. A moral comment.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: ונבלה is 'let us confuse'; the נ is the plural prefix, and the final ה is superfluous, like the ה of נרדה.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: one would ask for a brick and the other would bring clay, and the first would stand over him and split his skull. A midrash on 'not understand'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it is God's speech with the angels.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the grammarians derive ונבלה from the nifal; he rejects it, and takes נבלה as hifil from בלל, like ונעשה, on the evidence of 11:9. Some say their hearts were turned to hate one another so that each made up a language; others that He made them forget; he prefers that they were scattered and over the years the first language was forgotten.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'will not understand' means 'will not understand in the heart'; cf. 'a nation whose language you will not hear' (Deut 28:49).

Apparatus:

- Radak: the plural speech is only a figure; the Creator does not take counsel with the created (cf. Isa 40:14).
- Onkelos: 'come, let us reveal ourselves and confuse their language there'.

- עַל־כֵּן is a stock phrase introducing an explanation of a name or custom: 'therefore'.
- קָרָא has no stated subject; the 3rd masculine singular is impersonal, so 'its name was called'. Ibn Ezra and Radak do not change this.
- The etiology rests on wordplay: בָּבֶל (Babel) and בָּלַל (confuse). The verb בָּלַל is a Qal perfect, 'he confused'. Ibn Ezra and Radak analyse the name as בָּא בַּל, 'confusion came'.
- שְׂפַת כָּל־הָאָרֶץ: 'the lip of all the earth' means the one speech of 11:1, here 'the language of all the earth'.
- The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ divides the verse in two: the first half gives the name and its reason (כִּי־שָׁם בָּלַל, 'because there he confused'), the second the scattering (וּמִשָּׁם הֱפִיצָם, 'and from there he scattered them'). The fronted adverbs שָׁם and מִשָּׁם make a pair: 'there ... and from there'.

Note: שָׂפָה is rendered 'language' because 11:1 says the whole earth had one שָׂפָה and its דְּבָרִים, and Radak reads שְׂפַת as the tongues of the nations. 'Therefore its name was called' renders the impersonal active קָרָא.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'and from there He scattered them' teaches that they have no share in the world to come. He asks which was worse, the generation of the flood or that of the dispersion, who stretched out a hand against the Root (God) to make war on Him; yet the first were swept away and the second were not destroyed. The answer: the flood generation were robbers with strife among them, while these kept love and fellowship, as it says 'one language and one set of words'; so you learn that dissension is hateful (שֶׁשָּׂנְאוּי הַמַּחֲלֹקֶת) and peace is great. This is homily and does not bear on the English.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: בָּבֶל is two words, בָּא בַּל ('confusion came'), with the aleph of בָּא missing; so also בגד (30:11, for בָּא גָד) and בָּמָה (as if בָּא מָה). The English line keeps the name Babel; the derivation is recorded in the gloss and notes and agrees with the text's link to בָּלַל.
- Radak (records): Radak: He scattered most of them, since they divided into seventy languages and the one original language remained there; because the confusion happened there, the city is named Babel.
- Radak (records): Radak: one would expect the name to be בַּלֵּל, from בָּלַל; instead it is compounded of two words to bring out the sense more fully, בָּא בַּל, 'confusion came' upon them from heaven. בַּל is a noun from the full root בָּלַל, like קַן from קָנַן and חַן from חָנַן. The English follows the connection with בָּלַל given in the text, which Radak's analysis keeps.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders בָּלַל by בַּלְבֵּל and הֱפִיצָם by בַּדָּרִנּוּן; no variant in the Hebrew is recorded.
- Paragraph mark פ follows the verse.

- אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת opens a new section of the book, here the line of Shem down to Abram.
- The name שֵׁם is repeated: first as genitive of the heading, then as subject of a new nominal clause. The zaqef qaton on the first שֵׁם closes the heading; the yetiv, a disjunctive accent set before the word, stands on אֵלֶּה and on the second שֵׁם, at the head of each part.
- בֶּן־מְאַת שָׁנָה: age is expressed as 'son of N years', with the number in the construct state.
- וַיּוֹלֶד is Hifil wayyiqtol of יָלַד: the father is the subject, 'he fathered'. It continues the age clause: when he was a hundred, he fathered.

On the face of 5:32 and 7:6 (Noah 500 when he fathered his sons, 600 at the flood) Shem would be a hundred at the flood, not two years after it. Ibn Ezra refers the explanation of שְׁנָתַיִם to 10:21, 'the brother of Japheth the elder': Japheth was the first-born and Shem was born later. Radak says he explained it at 5:32.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'כשהוליד את ארפכשד שנתים אחר המבול': Shem was a hundred years old when he fathered Arpachshad, two years after the flood.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the explanation of שְׁנָתַיִם is given at 10:21, 'the brother of Japheth the elder' (Shem was not the first-born). He then reckons the lifespans: Shem lived 500 years after the flood, Arpachshad 438, Shelah 433, Eber 464, while Peleg lived only 239, half his fathers' years, so Peleg may have been named on the day he was gathered (died). He rejects the view that the tower's builders were seventy, matching seventy languages: Caphtorim and Pathrusim are not individuals, Noah and his sons are not counted, and by Seder Olam the builders were thousands and myriads. This does not alter the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: we would not know when Arpachshad was born, since Elam and Asshur were born first; the numbering gives the years from creation.

- Paragraph break not marked after this verse.

- The wayyiqtol וַיְחִי־ is the short form of יִחְיֶה: the III-he verb drops its final ־ֶה after the wayyiqtol prefix. It carries the narrative on from the preceding genealogy.
- שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה: seventy takes a singular noun; the etnaḥta on שָׁנָה ends the first half of the verse.
- וַיּוֹלֶד is the Hifil wayyiqtol of ילד, 'he caused to bear', that is, 'he fathered'.
- The three sons are listed with אֶת־ before each; the order does not say who was eldest, and the verse does not date the births of Nahor and Haran.

Note: The verse gives Terah's age at the first birth in the list, as the preceding verses do for earlier fathers. Abram is first in the list by importance, not necessarily by birth.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: Abram was born in the place called Ur Kasdim (compare בָּאֻרִים, Isaiah 24:15). Most likely the place had another name then, since the Chaldeans (כַּשְׂדִּים) descend from Nahor, Abram's brother; Moses wrote the name known in his own day. The proof that Abram was born there is that Haran his brother died there, in 'the land of his birth'. Or Ur may be a fire (אוּר) the Chaldeans made at that place, as in 'whose fire is in Zion' (Isaiah 31:9).
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Targum Onkelos renders the verse closely, with the same names and the same seventy years; it adds nothing to the sense.

#### Genesis 11:27

**These are the generations of Terah: Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran, and Haran fathered Lot.**

Grammar:

- וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת is the heading formula of Genesis; the account that follows is of what came from Terah, and the sons and Lot are its content.
- תֶּרַח is repeated (the yetiv on the second): the name stands as the subject of the following clause.
- The perfect הוֹלִיד (not wayyiqtol) restates 11:26 as a summary under the heading.
- וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת־לוֹט: the clause is added to name Lot, whose line matters to the story that follows.

Note: The English follows the commentators' sense that the heading opens the family account of Terah, who is its apparent subject. 'Generations' keeps the standard sense of תּוֹלְדֹת; the lexicon glosses it 'account of a man and his descendants'.

Commentary:

- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the verse before already named the sons, so the heading adds the events that befell Terah: the death of his son in his lifetime, his departure from Ur, and his death in Haran.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: Nahor's descendants are not listed because he did not beget until after the binding of Isaac; Haran's are, because Lot went with Abraham.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Targum Onkelos follows the Hebrew word for word.

**Haran died in the lifetime of his father Terah, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.**

Literal: and-died Haran upon face-of Terah his-father in-land-of his-birth in-Ur Chaldeans

| הָרָ֔ן | Haran | הָרָן |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| עַל | on | עַל | עלה | preposition | II.6 |
| פְּנֵ֖י | the face of — construct plural: 'before' in an idiom | פָּנֶה | פנה | noun (common, both genders, plural, construct) | I.6 |
| תֶּ֣רַח | Terah | תֶּ֫רַח |  | noun (proper name) |  |

| בְּאֶ֥רֶץ | in the land of — preposition with a construct noun | ב: in, with, by + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | preposition + noun (common, both genders, singular, construct) | 2 |
| מוֹלַדְתּ֖וֹ | his birth — a noun from ילד: 'birth, kindred' | מוֹלֶ֫דֶת | ילד | noun (common, feminine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| בְּא֥וּר | in Ur | ב: in, with, by + אוּר |  | preposition + noun (proper name) |  |
| כַּשְׂדִּֽים׃ | of the Chaldeans | כַּשְׂדִּים |  | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- עַל־פְּנֵי is an idiom: 'in the presence of', so 'during his life'; cf. Numbers 3:4 where Nadab and Abihu die עַל־פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן.
- The etnaḥta on אָבִיו marks the main division: the death and its time are set apart from the place.
- מוֹלַדְתּוֹ is a noun with a suffix, 'his kindred' or 'his birth'; it names the place of birth, 'the land of his birth'.
- The verb comes first, as in every wayyiqtol clause (וַיָּמׇת הָרָן, 'and-died Haran'); the English puts the subject first. וַיָּמׇת is the short Qal wayyiqtol of the hollow root מות: the stress moves back to the prefix (the munaḥ on יָּ) and the last vowel shortens to qamets ḥatuf, against the long form יָמוּת.

Note: The English follows Rashi, who takes עַל־פְּנֵי as 'in the lifetime of' his father (so Radak, citing Numbers 3:4). Ibn Ezra reads 'before his father', who saw him die; that reading is recorded. The midrash that Haran died by his father's doing (Rashi) is recorded, not adopted. 'Ur' is a proper name here; Menahem's reading 'valley' and the midrash's 'fire' are recorded in the commentary.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: עַל פְּנֵי is 'in his father's lifetime'; the aggadic midrash that Haran died through his father (the furnace story, Bereshit Rabbah) is a homily and he cites Menahem's reading of אוּר as 'a valley'. The English adopts the plain 'lifetime'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: עַל פְּנֵי means 'before (לִפְנֵי) his father': Haran died while his father looked on, as in Numbers 3:4, עַל פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֲבִיהֶם. The English 'in the lifetime of' follows Rashi; Ibn Ezra's 'in his father's sight' is recorded.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: he cites Rashi's midrash of the furnace and holds the tradition true, with אוּר as 'fire'. But Abraham was not born in Chaldea. Terah's family was from Aram, across the River (Joshua 24:2-3), where Abram and Nahor were born; Terah then went to Chaldea, where his youngest son Haran was born. So 'the land of his birth, Ur of the Chaldeans' is Haran's birthplace alone. In Ur, Abram was saved by a miracle, either hidden or open (the furnace); 15:7 'who brought you out of Ur' implies it.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'in his lifetime', as in Numbers 3:4.
- Radak (records): Radak: the place is called Ur of the Chaldeans by the name it bears 'today', in the writer's time. In Haran's time Kesed, whose sons were called Chaldeans, had not yet been born.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Targum Onkelos: 'in the presence of Terah his father, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans'.

Grammar:

- The verb וַיִּקַּח is singular though it has two subjects, because it agrees with the nearer one, Abram; Radak compares Exodus 7:10.
- נָשִׁים is the irregular plural of אִשָּׁה; the root listed is אנש.
- שֵׁם אֵשֶׁת־אַבְרָם שָׂרָי: the construct chain 'the name of the wife of Abram' is followed by the name in apposition.
- בַּת־הָרָן אֲבִי־מִלְכָּה וַאֲבִי יִסְכָּה: 'father of Milcah and father of Iscah' stands in apposition to הָרָן, bound to it by the conjunctive merkha on הָרָן; the English opens it with 'who was'. Radak explains why 'father of' follows 'daughter of': 11:27 named only Lot as Haran's child, so the verse adds that Haran also fathered Milcah and Iscah.

Note: The final clause is read as 'Haran, who was the father of Milcah and Iscah'. Whether Iscah is another name for Sarah is a question the commentators discuss; the English leaves the name as it stands. Sarai is the form of the name until 17:15.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: Iscah is Sarah, so called because she saw (סוֹכָה) by the holy spirit and because all gazed (סוֹכִין) at her beauty; also יִסְכָּה speaks of princeliness (נְסִיכוּת), as שָׂרָה speaks of rule (שְׂרָרָה). The English keeps the name Iscah and records the identification.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: Nahor's wife is named to give the descent of Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. The ancients said Iscah is Sarah; if that is a tradition, we accept it. Those who say Abraham, not Sarah, was barren contradict the text (Ishmael, Keturah's sons). He rejects the view that Sarah was Abram's sister. He also doubts she was Lot's sister, for then 11:31 would call her Terah's daughter, or his son's daughter as it does Lot. His own view is that the call of 12:1 came before 'Terah took' (11:31), since the Torah is not always in chronological order; so Terah set out 'to go to the land of Canaan', then liked Haran, settled there and died. The English leaves the identification open.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the wives are named in honor of Abram, and from Milcah came Rebecca.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the word 'father' is added after 'daughter' to say Haran also had other children.
- Radak (records): Radak: Iscah is Sarah (Sanhedrin 69), as shown by 'my sister, daughter of my father' in 20:12.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Targum Onkelos follows the Hebrew order and sense.

- אֵין followed by ל is the Hebrew way to say 'has not': 'there is not to her a child'.
- וָלָד is a rare noun for offspring, formed from ילד like the verbs of begetting above; Radak gives its pattern as that of חָכָם.
- The accents: etnaḥta on עֲקָרָה divides the verse into the state of Sarai and its consequence.

Note: The sentence is a plain statement. The English keeps the Hebrew's two clauses, the second restating the first in negative terms.

Commentary:

- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: it says Sarai was barren to show the miracle that she bore, and in that miracle another, that she was ninety; Milcah, by contrast, was not barren but delayed by an accidental illness.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: she had none while in Ur of the Chaldeans, but in Canaan she did, as God promised Abraham in 12:2.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: וָלָד is a noun on the pattern of חָכָם.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Targum Onkelos: 'and Sarai was barren, she had no child'.
